lead.title: Only 2.36 per cent of nannies will work a rotation, and the families who move the most are the ones who cannot fill the post
lead.standfirst: The scarcest people in private service are not the most senior, they are the ones willing to live out of a suitcase.
lead.body:
Morgan & Mallet has published its Household Staff Annual Report 2025/26, drawn from a database of more than 50,300 candidates and from placements made across the United States, the United Kingdom, Europe and the Middle East between January 2024 and October 2025. Buried in the childcare section is a figure that explains why certain posts stay open for months while others fill in a fortnight. Only 2.36 per cent of the nannies on the agency's books will work a rotational schedule, and only 4.82 per cent will travel regularly. Every other candidate is looking for one house, one city and one set of school runs.

Scarcity of that order has a price, and the Gulf pays it. The United Arab Emirates now compensates travelling nannies more generously than any other market in the world, from AED 300,000 to AED 600,000, which the agency converts to as much as USD 163,200 a year. The United States follows at up to USD 150,000, the United Kingdom at up to USD 145,200 and Switzerland at up to USD 132,022. Morgan & Mallet expects Gulf pay for the role to reach USD 180,000 to USD 190,000. Set against a nanny who stays put in France, where the range tops out near USD 67,200, the premium is not being paid for childcare. It is being paid for a strong passport, an unencumbered diary and a willingness to be on an aircraft on Thursday.

The travelling brief is also a short one. Rotational placements typically run from 6 to 12 months before converting into a permanent governess post or a hybrid role, which means the family is back in the market inside a year. The candidates who thrive treat mobility as a documented competence rather than an accident of circumstance: 82 per cent of the agency's Los Angeles candidates for travelling work list domestic and international travel, private aviation included, as an explicit part of their offer.

Underneath the childcare numbers sits a structural change that reaches every role in the house. Average service in a private household has fallen from roughly twenty years to roughly three. Families still working to the old assumption that a post takes 2 to 3 months to fill are now advised to allow 4 to 6. Given that ultra-high-net-worth families commonly keep three to five homes, and that most estate managers run at least three properties at once, the rotation problem is not really a childcare problem. It is the shape of the modern household, and it is arriving at every door in the service wing.
lead.why: The best paid roles in private service are the ones that ask a candidate to be mobile. Rotation experience, travel documents and private aviation familiarity are assets that can be built deliberately, and they now separate a shortlist from a placement.
lead.src: Morgan & Mallet, Household Staff Annual Report 2025/26

articles.title: European business jet flying falls for the first time in fourteen months, while the rest of the world keeps climbing
articles.body:
Argus International's July traffic figures, reported on 11 August, put global business aviation flight activity 5.6 per cent above the same month last year. The headline conceals a split. Europe recorded a decline of 1.2 per cent against July 2025, its first annual contraction in fourteen months, while North America powered the global increase, with turboprops leading the surge there.

The European weakness is concentrated at the top of the market. Large cabin flights across Europe fell 6.5 per cent year on year. That is precisely the tier that carries a principal and an entourage between London, Geneva, Nice and the Gulf without a technical stop, and it is the tier a household is most likely to be arranging on a family's behalf in August. Smaller aircraft held their ground more comfortably.

A single month is not a trend, and July 2025 was an unusually strong comparison. But the direction matters for anyone who books aircraft. When large cabin demand in Europe softens, availability improves and repositioning becomes easier to negotiate late, which is the opposite of the picture in North America, where activity is still climbing and short notice lift remains hard to secure.
articles.why: Anyone who arranges private lift for a family is negotiating against the traffic curve. Knowing which cabin class is loosening in which region is the difference between accepting the first quotation and asking for a better one.

articles.title: Riyadh acquires an ultra-prime address built around large plots, gated enclaves and staff quarters
articles.body:
Wadi Safar, a low density residential district inside the Diriyah masterplan roughly twenty kilometres west of central Riyadh, has emerged as the Saudi capital's first genuinely ultra-prime address. Diriyah is the heritage site recognised as the birthplace of the first Saudi state, and the district around it is being developed as a private estate community with championship golf, five star hospitality and residential plots sized for mansions rather than villas.

Four distinct offerings have been launched within the district: Rayana Mansions, Trump Mansions at Rayana, Altara Diriyah Wadi Safar and Amara Diriyah Wadi Safar. Rayana Mansions is marketed as trophy housing inside a gated enclave, aimed at Saudi families, Gulf investors and international buyers, and is designed explicitly for multi-generational living, with privacy, staff accommodation and entertaining space named as the organising principles. Altara sells land to buyers who intend to commission their own house. Amara offers a dual mansion format, two separate residences on a single large plot, for extended families or for guests who need full residential function rather than a spare room.

The supply model is deliberately restrictive: large plots, gated enclaves, controlled release, a pattern borrowed from Emirates Hills and the Palm Jumeirah villa communities in Dubai, where scarcity of land rather than volume of construction did the work of establishing prestige. Riyadh's own demand base is domestic before it is international. Saudi family offices and high-net-worth individuals form the core of the buyer pool, supplemented by Gulf and international capital, while the regional headquarters programme has pushed a new layer of executive housing demand into the city.

For the private service reader, the significant detail is not the golf course. It is that staff accommodation and entertaining capacity are being designed into these houses at the plan stage rather than retrofitted, and that the dual mansion format implies two households under one ownership, with guest wings that operate independently. Houses of that shape do not run on two people. They run on a structured team with written protocol, and they are being built now.
articles.why: A new ultra-prime district is a new employment market. Houses designed from the outset around staff quarters, guest wings and multi-generational occupancy require larger teams and clearer lines of authority than the villa stock they are replacing.

articles.title: The London art season opens in a public park in September and peaks in The Regent's Park in October
articles.body:
Frieze London and Frieze Masters return to The Regent's Park from 14 to 18 October, running side by side across a single site, one fair devoted to contemporary work and the other spanning several millennia of art history. This year's curated sections carry 50 presentations, given over to young galleries and to artists showing in London for the first time, which is where dealers and advisers look first for the names that will move in price before the winter sales.

The season in fact opens a month earlier and costs nothing to attend. Frieze Sculpture occupies the English Gardens of The Regent's Park from 16 September to 1 November, free and outdoors, with eleven international artists including Angel Otero, Conrad Shawcross, Tarini Sethi and Ivana Basic. It runs for six and a half weeks, which makes it one of the few fixtures in the London cultural calendar a household can build into a visiting principal's diary without a ticket, an invitation or a queue.

October in London is a week when the private diary compresses. Principals fly in for the fairs and stay for the auctions that cluster around them, houses fill with guests, private views and dinners land on consecutive evenings, and a car is needed in Regent's Park at hours when Regent's Park is difficult. The dates are published in June for a reason. The households that read them in August are the ones that are not improvising in October.
articles.why: Cultural fluency in private service is practical before it is decorative. Knowing when the fairs open, what is free and what requires an invitation is how a house manager anticipates a principal's autumn rather than reacting to it.

briefs.b: The Monaco Yacht Show holds its 35th edition in Port Hercule from 23 to 26 September, with a fleet expected to reach 120 yachts by opening day, 43 of them delivered during 2026. The organisers note that build slots at leading yards are now committed through 2028 and 2029, which makes a hull delivering this year one of the scarcer commodities in the market.

Demand for private chefs is concentrated in five markets. The United States accounts for 35 per cent of global requests, the United Arab Emirates and the wider Middle East for 20 per cent, France and Monaco for 20 per cent, Switzerland for 15 per cent and the United Kingdom for 10 per cent. In Los Angeles, 41 per cent of placed chefs hold certification in nutrition alongside their culinary qualification.
briefs.src: Morgan & Mallet, Household Staff Annual Report 2025/26

briefs.b: In France, 21 per cent of the agency's clients over the past year asked for a domestic couple and could not find one, making it the most persistently unfilled brief in that market. In the United States, estate manager requests account for 10 per cent of the total, and half of all estate manager posts worldwide sit in American households.
briefs.src: Morgan & Mallet, Household Staff Annual Report 2025/26

briefs.t: USD 18 trillion of it to charity
briefs.b: Of the USD 124 trillion expected to change hands in the United States through 2048, USD 105 trillion goes to heirs and USD 18 trillion goes to charity. More than half of the total, USD 62 trillion, comes from high-net-worth and ultra-high-net-worth households, who make up only 2 per cent of all households.

lead.title: Discretion appears in 61.3 per cent of American household briefs, three times more often than any qualification
lead.standfirst: A new study of 465 United States staffing briefs finds that families write down trust and private household experience far more often than a certificate, and that the roles carrying the widest remit ask for the longest record.
lead.body:
Morgan & Mallet published on 18 August the fullest picture yet of what American families actually write down when they ask an agency to find someone. The firm analysed 465 United States job briefs recorded between May 2022 and June 2026, each one a client's request to recruit for a single role. The single most frequent requirement was not a skill at all. Discretion or confidentiality appeared in 61.3 per cent of briefs. Previous private household experience followed at 58.5 per cent. A formal qualification or certification appeared in 20.4 per cent, roughly a third as often as discretion.

The practical skills sit underneath that. Laundry and ironing appeared in 43.2 per cent of briefs, cooking in 41.3 per cent, events and entertaining in 31.6 per cent. The ordering matters more than the individual figures. A family can teach a house its own way of pressing a shirt. It cannot teach judgment, and it cannot un-hear a conversation that left the property. The report's authors put it plainly: skills help someone carry out the role, while trust and an understanding of family life let them complete the work without adding to the family's mental load.

Experience requirements climb with responsibility rather than with prestige. Across the roles measured, families asked for a minimum of four years. Butler and formal service briefs carried the highest average minimum at 6.7 years, followed by household and estate management at 6.3 years, then nanny and childcare at 4.7 years, transport at 4.6 years and housekeeping at 4.5 years. These are the positions where someone welcomes guests, leads a team, coordinates contractors and keeps the house running while the principals are elsewhere, and the length of record families ask for reflects exactly that.

A smaller set of briefs asks for something narrower still. Fine dining or Michelin kitchen experience appeared in 7.5 per cent, yacht experience in 5.2 per cent, formal or silver service in 3.7 per cent, Montessori training in 2.2 per cent and smart home systems in 1.3 per cent. These requirements are rare across the whole sample but decisive for the household that writes them, because they define the entire search. A candidate who holds one of them holds a key to a very small door.

The methodology is worth stating, since the numbers will be quoted loosely elsewhere. The data covers one agency's American assignments, and a brief records a client's request rather than a confirmed placement. It is not a census of every private household in the United States. It is, however, an unusually direct record of what families say they want before anyone has been interviewed.
lead.why: The list of requirements is effectively the order in which a candidate should build a career: discretion and private household experience first, technical skills second, certificates third. A qualification opens a conversation. A record of confidentiality is what keeps the post.
lead.src: Morgan & Mallet, Inside the Modern Private Household, US Household Staffing Report 2026

articles.title: The Hamptons sells 378 houses in a quarter, 21 per cent fewer than last year, and the median price still rises by almost a third
articles.body:
The second quarter figures for the East End describe a market that is contracting in volume and expanding in price at the same time. A total of 378 properties changed hands between April and June, a fall of 21.1 per cent on the same period in 2025. Total dollar volume came in at approximately USD 1.45 billion, down 11.9 per cent. On those two numbers alone the season looks weak.

The price data says the opposite. The average sale price rose 11.7 per cent year on year to USD 3.84 million. The median rose far harder, up 31.9 per cent to USD 2.5 million. When the median climbs three times faster than the average, the explanation is usually compositional rather than inflationary: the cheaper transactions have stopped happening, so the middle of the market has moved up the ladder rather than the ladder itself moving.

That is precisely what the report describes. The shortage is concentrated below USD 3 million, where there is very little to buy, while activity above USD 3 million has held up and carried the quarter. Fewer closings, not falling values. The East End has also been changing character for some years, as New York families who once treated a Hamptons house as a summer address now keep it as a primary or year-round residence.

For anyone who runs a house out there, the second point is the operational one. A seasonal property is opened in May and closed in October, and its staffing follows that rhythm. A year-round property needs heating plant that works in February, a contractor list that answers in the off season, a security arrangement for an empty house in midwinter and a household team that is not hired on a summer contract. The transition from one model to the other is rarely announced. It is discovered by whoever is holding the keys in January.
articles.why: A market where houses are held longer and used year round changes the shape of the job attached to them, from a seasonal opening and closing to a permanent operation with winter maintenance, off-season contractors and a team that does not disperse in September.
articles.src: Hamptons Prive, on the Brown Harris Stevens Hamptons second quarter 2026 market report

articles.title: The family office moves towards lean structures and direct ownership, and the house is expected to feel as frictionless as the portfolio
articles.body:
Knight Frank's 2026 Family Office Survey, published in April as part of the twentieth edition of The Wealth Report, draws on interviews with more than 40 family offices in London, New York, Dubai, Singapore, Hong Kong and beyond. The sector it describes is growing quickly and remains remarkably varied in how it operates, but the direction of travel is towards structure: explicit targets, formal processes and decisions taken on analysis rather than instinct.

Three changes sit underneath that. Co-investment is spreading, letting offices share risk and reach larger opportunities than they could alone. Professionalisation is advancing, with many offices now employing internal specialists in private equity, venture capital and real estate rather than outsourcing the judgment. And portfolios keep widening, combining liquid assets with private equity, venture capital, infrastructure and direct property. Direct ownership of real estate remains attractive precisely because it lets a family shape a development strategy and keep the whole of the upside instead of sharing it through a fund.

The survey also records a preference the household will feel directly. Knight Frank calls it frictionless wealth: a move towards lighter, more flexible structures, mirroring a broader shift in ultra-wealthy life towards convenience and immediacy. Several offices are applying the same principle internally, keeping the permanent team small and buying in outside expertise when an opportunity appears. A rising generation wants to see its positions live, daily, with currency overlay, rather than in a quarterly pack.

London appears in the survey as a city under pressure rather than a city in decline. Sentiment is more cautious than it was a decade ago, yet almost nobody interviewed expects the city's importance to disappear, and its financial depth, connectivity and time zone remain powerful anchors in an era when families keep several bases at once. Dubai, Hong Kong and Singapore are gaining ground alongside New York, not instead of London.

A lean office has a consequence that rarely appears in the research. When the permanent headcount is deliberately small, the work does not vanish. It settles on whoever is closest to the principal and already trusted, which in practice means the house manager, the estate manager or the senior assistant. The frictionless family is frictionless because someone absorbs the friction.
articles.why: Smaller, flatter family offices push more coordination onto the household team. The person running the house increasingly holds tasks that a larger office would have kept in-house, which raises both the standard expected and the value of the post.
articles.src: Knight Frank, Family Office Survey 2026, The Wealth Report

articles.title: Cannes opens the autumn season on 8 September with around 700 boats and 150 world premieres
articles.body:
The Cannes Yachting Festival returns for its 49th edition from 8 to 13 September, opening the international boating season two weeks before Monaco. More than 680 exhibitors are expected, with a fleet of roughly 700 boats from 5 to 50 metres, and around 150 world premieres. It remains Europe's leading in-water show and the principal fixture for vessels of 500 gross tonnes and below.

The layout is unchanged in principle and matters for anyone arranging a client's visit. The Vieux Port takes the motor segment, from 12 to 50 metres, together with superyachts, rigid inflatables and catamarans, with large yachts on the Quai Max Laubeuf and the redesigned Jetee holding in-water yachts and engine manufacturers. Port Canto takes sail above 10 metres, the brokerage fleet, smaller motorboats and the water toys area. A regular maritime shuttle runs between the two, which is the detail that decides whether an afternoon of appointments is feasible or not.

The 2026 edition is the first under Constance Brement, a new director drawn from the nautical and luxury sectors, whose stated aim is to widen the show's international reach and improve the visitor experience. The programme leans hard on the energy transition. The Innovation Route runs a dedicated trail through efficiency, sustainability and propulsion, judged by an international panel of professionals and journalists, with awards for navigation equipment, sustainable products, innovative boats and corporate responsibility. The finalists of the Best of Boat Awards are announced on 9 September at six in the evening.

Cannes is the show where a family that charters decides what it wants to charter next, and where a first boat is often bought. For the household side, September in the Riviera means diaries that fill in fifteen minute blocks, tender movements between two ports, and a week in which the principal's schedule is set by a shuttle timetable rather than by the house.
articles.why: Boat show weeks are among the densest logistical periods in the private calendar. Knowing which port holds which segment, and that a shuttle links them, is the difference between a schedule that works and one that collapses by mid-morning.

articles.title: Frieze Seoul opens its fifth edition on 2 September with more than 125 galleries, and Asia keeps the first week of the art year
articles.body:
Frieze Seoul returns to COEX in Gangnam from 2 to 5 September, in partnership with Kiaf SEOUL. The fifth edition brings together more than 125 galleries from 30 countries, with over 70 per cent of participants based across the Asia-Pacific region and more than 50 exhibitors holding permanent spaces in Seoul itself. The Galleries section alone gathers over 85 international houses, among them Hauser & Wirth, Pace, White Cube, David Zwirner, Lisson, Thaddaeus Ropac, Gladstone, Lehmann Maupin and Sprueth Magers, alongside the leading Korean names including Kukje, Gallery Hyundai, PKM, Arario and Hakgojae.

Two curated sections are new this year. Material Practice, curated by Hyeyoung Cho, sits at the intersection of contemporary art and design and draws on Seoul's traditions of craft and material innovation. Spotlight, curated by Wonseok Koh, arrives at Frieze Seoul for the first time and is devoted to solo presentations of twentieth century artists, foregrounding overlooked figures and art-historical narratives outside the dominant Western canon. Focus, now in its fourth year and advised by Seolhui Lee, presents 16 galleries founded in or after 2014, and expands beyond Asia for the first time.

The fair is only part of the week. Neighborhood Nights run from 31 August to 3 September, moving each evening through a different district: Euljiro on the Monday, Hannam on the Tuesday, Cheongdam on the Wednesday and Samcheong on the Thursday, with late openings, performances and events. Museum programming across the city includes Koo Jeong A at the Leeum Museum of Art, Do Ho Suh at MMCA Seoul, Sol LeWitt at the Amorepacific Museum of Art and Es Devlin at FUTURA Seoul. Deutsche Bank continues as global lead partner, in the 23rd year of that arrangement.

The practical shape of the week is the point. A principal who attends is not attending a fair, but a five day itinerary spread across four districts, with invitation-only hours on the Wednesday, preview access on the Thursday morning and public opening only from three in the afternoon on that day. Anyone building the diary needs to know which door opens at which hour, because at Frieze the difference between the preview and the public opening is the difference between seeing a work and reading about it.
articles.why: Cultural fluency is not knowing that a fair exists but knowing how its week is structured. Preview tiers, neighbourhood evenings and museum openings are the raw material of a well-built diary for a collecting family.

articles.title: Three states hold almost two thirds of American household briefs, and the Florida hiring season starts this month
articles.body:
The same Morgan & Mallet analysis maps where the American work actually sits, and the concentration is severe. California accounted for 24.1 per cent of United States briefs, Florida for 23.0 per cent and New York for 16.1 per cent, with a clear drop to Texas and Georgia behind them. Yet New York City, Miami and Los Angeles together made up only 33.8 per cent of briefs. Two thirds of the searches happen somewhere other than the three obvious cities.

The list of top locations makes the point. Braselton in Georgia came fourth, ahead of San Francisco, and recorded the largest increase in share of any city in 2025, rising 8.0 percentage points against the 2023 to 2024 period. Belle Vernon in Pennsylvania, Palm Beach, Tampa, Greenwich and Washington DC completed the top ten. Within the leading states the settings vary enormously, from Malibu and Atherton to Jupiter Island, East Hampton and Old Westbury. Household staffing follows the properties a family uses, not the cities a map would suggest.

The working arrangements are less uniform than the trade assumes. Of briefs that specified an employment basis, 95.2 per cent were full time, and where permanence was stated, 93.3 per cent sought a permanent hire. Living arrangements split three ways: 39.6 per cent live-in, 32.5 per cent live-out and 28.0 per cent open to either. In New York in particular, families increasingly prefer live-out staff, because apartment space is scarce and a local who already knows the city is more useful than one who needs housing.

Season matters more than most candidates realise. Florida's hiring runs opposite to the north east, because the snowbird households arriving from Massachusetts, New York, Connecticut and Canada need to be staffed by October. The recruitment high season there therefore begins in August and September, which is to say now. Staff rotate between properties and follow the principals, so a candidate willing to move with a household has a market that reopens twice a year rather than once.

Two structural facts sit behind all of it. Estate managers account for roughly one in ten American requests and remain among the hardest posts to fill, in part because the estate manager usually goes on to build the rest of the team. And average tenure in private service has fallen from around 20 years to nearer three, which means the candidate who can show five years or more with one family now stands out rather than blends in.
articles.why: Knowing the geography and the calendar of demand is a hiring advantage in itself. A candidate who understands that Florida staffs up in late summer, and that half the work sits outside the famous cities, can time an approach rather than wait for one.
articles.src: Morgan & Mallet, US Household Staffing Report 2026 and 2026 US salary guidance

briefs.b: Global Jet Capital's second quarter market brief puts business jet availability at 6.6 per cent of the fleet, down from 6.7 per cent in the first quarter and well below the historical average of roughly 10 per cent. Listings rose 3.3 per cent year on year, but the growth came from older aircraft while supply of jets aged 12 years and under tightened further. Departures rose 3.4 per cent across the first half, led by fractional operators.
briefs.src: GlobalAir, on Global Jet Capital data, 19 August 2026

briefs.b: Frieze confirmed this month that Frieze Seoul will move from COEX to the Dongdaemun Design Plaza from 2027. The 2026 edition is therefore the last at the Gangnam venue that has hosted the fair since it launched. Anyone planning a family's art calendar beyond this year should note the change of district.

Where an American brief specified a language, English appeared in 75.8 per cent of them. French followed at 26.8 per cent and Spanish at 25.5 per cent, with Italian at 7.2 per cent. Families often ask for more than one, so the figures overlap, and a second language remains one of the cheapest differentiators a candidate can hold.
briefs.src: Morgan & Mallet, US Household Staffing Report 2026

briefs.b: Butler and formal service briefs carried the highest average minimum experience requirement of any role measured, at 6.7 years, ahead of household and estate management at 6.3 years. Nanny and childcare briefs asked for 4.7 years, transport 4.6 and housekeeping 4.5. Across all roles the floor sat at about four years.
briefs.src: Morgan & Mallet, US Household Staffing Report 2026

lead.title: Swiss mountain property rises 6 per cent while the lakes reach a plateau, and the chalet stops being a seasonal house
lead.standfirst: The annual UBS study of Swiss luxury property finds Alpine prices climbing twice as fast as the national average, driven by foreign buyers who treat a chalet as a holding rather than a holiday.
lead.body:
UBS Chief Investment Office publishes an annual survey of the Swiss luxury property landscape, and the 2026 edition describes a market that has split in two. Across the 31 top locations the bank tracks, luxury prices rose by an average of just over 3 per cent in 2025. That was a slowdown on the previous year and, unusually, slightly weaker than price growth in the broader owner-occupied market. The mountains did not slow. Luxury prices in the Alpine resorts rose 6 per cent, faster than the year before, and the bank attributes the difference almost entirely to buyers from abroad.

The price levels are worth reading precisely, because they set the operating scale of the houses attached to them. St. Moritz is now the most expensive luxury location in Switzerland at an average of about CHF 52,000 per square metre. Gstaad and Verbier follow at roughly CHF 45,000. Outside the mountains the highest prices are on Lake Geneva, where Cologny averages CHF 43,000, and on Lake Zurich, where Küsnacht averages CHF 37,000. In practical terms, a 150 square metre apartment in a good position with a high specification costs from CHF 4 million to CHF 5 million, and a single family house standing on more than 1,000 square metres of land moves quickly past CHF 10 million.

Over the past five years, Swiss luxury prices have risen by just under 5 per cent a year on average, and mountain property is now around 40 per cent more expensive than it was five years ago, the strongest gain of any Swiss region. The bank puts much of this down to domestic wealth creation alongside foreign demand. Switzerland currently has about 50 per cent more taxpayers declaring assets above CHF 10 million than it did in 2019, an increase of nearly 10,000 people. Measured internationally, St. Moritz leads the ranking, Monaco is second and Aspen third, with average luxury prices in all three of at least USD 60,000 per square metre and six figure prices per square metre no longer uncommon in the best micro locations.

The outlook is the part that will shape hiring. UBS expects 2026 to be weaker than recent years. Slow economic conditions and declining affordability for luxury apartments in the mid single digit millions are likely to weigh on demand, and in the primary-home markets on Lake Geneva and Lake Zurich the bank believes a price plateau has already been reached in many places. The mountains are the exception it does not expect to reverse, because the buyers there are foreign, largely insensitive to price, and increasingly regard a vacation home as an investment asset. The strongest global gains in 2025 were recorded in the Middle East, but the bank expects demand to refocus on classic locations with high political stability, which keeps Switzerland at the front of the queue.
lead.why: A chalet held as an asset is kept ready rather than opened for a fortnight in February. That turns seasonal caretaking into year round household management, with permanent staff, standing supplier accounts and a house that must be presentable for a principal who may arrive at short notice, or not at all.
lead.src: UBS Chief Investment Office, Luxury Property Focus 2026

articles.title: Residential security in prime central London settles at £35,000 to £85,000 a year, and the house manager is the one who administers the contract
articles.body:
A market guide published in July by Priority First, a London building management and security firm, and updated at the beginning of August, puts a number on something the private house has been absorbing quietly. Comprehensive residential security in prime central London, meaning manned guarding, remote monitoring and integration with front of house, now costs from £35,000 to £85,000 a year. Properties in Mayfair, Belgravia and Knightsbridge are spending an average of £48,000. The market has grown markedly since 2023, and the firm notes that houses in the SW1, W1 and SW3 postcodes are disproportionately targeted because of perceived wealth concentration.

The largest component is people, not hardware. A single officer on a 12 hour shift costs from £180 to £320, depending on experience and the level of vetting required. A house that wants a physical presence around the clock is therefore committing between £131,400 and £233,600 a year in staffing alone, before management overhead, training or relief cover for holiday and sickness. Mobile patrols, typically two to four visits a night, run from £3,600 to £7,200 a year and are treated as a supplement to a resident presence rather than a replacement for it.

Equipment is the smaller line. A full installation for a typical townhouse, covering perimeter detection, internal cameras, access control and alarms, costs from £25,000 to £65,000 to fit, with a further £4,800 to £9,600 a year for monitoring and maintenance and £6,000 to £15,000 for control room cover. Compliance sits on top of all of it. Every operative must hold a valid Security Industry Authority licence, and prime properties generally insist on BS7858 screening, which verifies five years of employment history alongside criminal record and credit checks. Cameras bring the house inside UK data protection law, with obligations on signage, retention periods and secure storage. Listed buildings add a further layer: Westminster's planning department reports that 43 per cent of security applications for Grade II listed properties require modification to meet heritage requirements.

The guide's working rule is 0.5 to 1.2 per cent of property value a year, weighted upward where a house holds a significant collection or accommodates a public figure. It also makes a point that will be familiar to anyone who has run a large household: security functions best when it is coordinated with maintenance and front of house rather than bought as an isolated service. Unlit paths, failed locks, compromised service entrances and overgrown planting that blocks a camera are found on maintenance rounds, not on patrol.
articles.why: Vetting files, licence expiry dates, control room escalation routes and visitor logs land on the desk of whoever runs the house. Reading a security quotation properly, and knowing which items sit outside the headline price, has become part of estate management rather than a specialism bought in.
articles.src: Priority First, Residential Security in Prime Central London 2026

articles.title: Pre-owned aircraft dealers close 746 transactions in six months, and the shelf a family buys from keeps getting shorter
articles.body:
The International Aircraft Dealers Association reported 746 pre-owned business aircraft transactions by its accredited members in the first half of 2026, an increase of 21 per cent on the same period last year. A further 536 aircraft were placed under acquisition agreements during the six months, up 8 per cent. The trade is not simply brokering other people's aeroplanes: dealers took 118 aircraft into their own inventory, an increase of 87 per cent year on year and twice the figure recorded in the first half of 2024.

The pricing signal runs the same way. Dealers reported 67 price reductions over the period, 11 per cent fewer than a year earlier and the smallest number since the association began tracking the measure in 2023. Buying aircraft onto your own balance sheet and cutting fewer asking prices are both statements of confidence about resale, and they are being made at the same time.

AMSTAT's analysis of the second quarter reaches the same conclusion from the supply side. Transactions rose 11.2 per cent year on year and ran about 14 per cent above the ten year average for the quarter, while listed turbine inventory finished June at 5.8 per cent of the active fleet, the lowest reading since February 2024 and well below the ten year norm of 7.2 per cent. For jets specifically the figure was 6.5 per cent against a norm of 8.1 per cent. The heavy jet segment, the category most relevant to long range private travel, was the strongest of all, with transactions up 43.8 per cent year on year.

A tight second hand market changes the arithmetic of ownership. A family that would once have traded up within a season now finds the aircraft it wants is not listed at all, and the choice narrows to waiting for a new delivery or keeping the existing aeroplane in service for longer than planned. Both outcomes push work back onto the household rather than the dealer.
articles.why: When an aircraft cannot be replaced quickly, the one the family already has must be kept flying. Maintenance windows, crew retention and charter fallback shift from occasional decisions into standing responsibilities for whoever coordinates the principal's movements.
articles.src: Corporate Jet Investor, on IADA and AMSTAT data

articles.title: Seven of the eight largest watch brands hold their value better than in the spring, and the secondary market finds a floor
articles.body:
The quarterly watch market review compiled by Morgan Stanley with WatchCharts, taken from a snapshot on 29 June 2026, found that seven of the eight brands it tracks improved their value retention against the first quarter. In plain terms, watches from those makers are being discounted less on the second hand market than they were three months earlier. After a long stretch in which the direction of travel was consistently downward, that is the first broad reversal in the data.

The movements themselves are modest. Secondary market prices rose quarter on quarter at Rolex, up 1.7 per cent, Patek Philippe, up 3.0 per cent, Cartier, up 1.9 per cent, and Omega, up 1.9 per cent. Nobody is describing this as a return to the conditions of 2021 and 2022, when waiting lists at authorised dealers were a form of currency. What has changed is that the secondary market has stopped acting as a discount channel for surplus supply.

Discontinuation still moves prices faster than anything else. Rolex confirmed at Watches and Wonders in 2026 that its Pepsi references were ending, and the stainless steel Ref. 126710BLRO gained close to 12 per cent in the first quarter, trading at around USD 22,500. Scarcity announced from the top of the house remains the most reliable driver of value in the category.

For a household, none of this is abstract. Watches are insured on scheduled valuations, carried between residences, occasionally worn to events that generate photographs, and periodically sold. A market that has stopped falling means replacement values quoted two years ago are now more likely to be too low than too high.
articles.why: Insurance schedules, travel inventories and safe records are usually maintained inside the house. When second hand values turn, the person keeping the collection log is the first to see that a valuation has gone stale and needs to be raised with the family office.
articles.src: WatchPro, on Morgan Stanley and WatchCharts data

briefs.b: The Monaco Yacht Show returns to Port Hercule from 23 to 26 September 2026 for its 35th edition, with more than 560 exhibitors expected by the opening. A new Designer Gallery, announced on 12 August, gives naval architects and interior designers a dedicated space alongside the shipyards, brokerage houses and management firms.

Global private jet departures passed 78,000 in the week ending 9 August 2026, an increase of 2.3 per cent on the same week last year and the first year on year gain in three weeks. A 4 per cent rise in United States flights carried the increase, returning the year to date trend to roughly 4 per cent ahead of 2025.

briefs.t: A third of family offices struggled to hire
briefs.b: Botoff Consulting's 2026 compensation and talent planning survey, drawing on 365 family offices, family investment firms and private trust companies, found that more than a third reported recruiting difficulties over the past year, with the larger offices reporting greater difficulty than the smaller ones. Total direct compensation rose meaningfully year on year for both executives and staff.

briefs.t: Four to six months to fill a post
briefs.b: Recruitment guidance for 2026 advises families to begin household searches four to six months ahead rather than the traditional two to three, and to budget 15 to 20 per cent above standard rates for candidates holding specialist qualifications. Hybrid posts such as family assistant and nanny housekeeper remain the fastest growing part of the market.

strap: A daily dispatch from the world you are entering

lead.title: Technology fluency becomes a condition of employment in the private house, and the households that pay the most now test for it
lead.standfirst: A recruiter's market note published this month argues that 2026 is the year technical proficiency stopped being a bonus in private service and became a threshold requirement.
lead.body: For most of the trade's history, technical competence in a private household meant the commercial washing machine, the oven timer and the boiler. That definition has collapsed. In a market note published on 11 August, the recruitment firm Achieve Hospitality sets out six technical competencies it now sees written into briefs for household roles: smart home system operation and first line troubleshooting, digital security and privacy protocol, household management software, multi property coordination and remote access, audiovisual and entertainment systems, and sustainability and energy management. The firm's position is blunt. Experience in private households, on its own, is no longer sufficient evidence of capability. The named systems matter, because they are what a candidate will be asked about. Automation in ultra high net worth residences runs largely on Crestron, Lutron, Control4 and Savant, controlling lighting, climate, entertainment and security across separate zones. Audiovisual sits on Sonos and Kaleidescape. Operations increasingly run on dedicated household platforms such as Household and Centriq, where work orders, vendor contacts, service histories and inventories are logged rather than passed along verbally between shifts. The expectation is not that the house manager becomes an engineer. It is that she operates the systems fluently, resolves the routine fault herself, knows the point at which a specialist is called, and can brief new staff on how the house actually works. The commercial backdrop explains the pressure. The Business Research Company puts the global private household services market at USD 351.99 billion in 2025 and USD 386.02 billion in 2026, a compound annual growth rate of 9.7 per cent. Families are running more properties in more jurisdictions, and a large number of principals converted seasonal residences into primary homes after the pandemic. Household teams now coordinate systems, security protocols and vendor programmes with a formality closer to a family office than to a traditional domestic roster. Complexity of that kind is not absorbed by goodwill. It is absorbed by documentation and by systems, and by the people who know how to use both. The money follows. Achieve Hospitality reports that estate managers with strong technology literacy are commanding salaries of GBP 80,000 and above in the United Kingdom and USD 100,000 and above in the United States, with senior multi property roles running well past that. House managers with documented smart home and digital management experience sit at the top of their bands. On the security side, the firm cites industry data showing that staff who sign non disclosure agreements and follow digital protocols earn 15 to 20 per cent more than those who do not. For candidates seeking a formal credential, the note points to the Level 3 Smart Home Technician apprenticeship standard published by Skills England as the framework employers recognise. The practical instruction concerns the curriculum vitae. A line reading familiar with smart home systems is treated as filler. What earns an interview is specific and countable: the platform named, the number of properties covered, the size of the team coordinated, the daily system checks and vendor liaison actually performed. Candidates are also advised to raise digital discretion directly at interview, setting out how household data, device policies and personal social media are handled, because that is the question the principal cares about most and rarely asks first.
lead.why: The technical layer of a house is now part of the job description rather than a curiosity, and it is priced. Documenting which systems you have run, across how many properties, is the fastest way to move up a pay band without changing employer.

articles.title: Prime central London records its 39th consecutive month of falling values, and transactions rise anyway
articles.body:
Knight Frank's latest reading of the capital's prime market, reported on 13 August, describes two things happening at once. Prime sales across London rose 14 per cent in the three months to July, and 3 per cent in prime central London. Yet average prices in prime central London fell 3.3 per cent in the year to July, the 39th consecutive month of annual decline, and now sit 23 per cent below their last peak in mid 2015.

The activity figures come with a caveat the agency states plainly. Exchanges were 7 per cent lower in both London and prime central London over the same three months, and against the five year average they are down 6 per cent across London and 15 per cent in the centre. Knight Frank notes that the comparison is distorted by successive stamp duty changes during and after the pandemic, and by the repricing of mortgage rates that began in 2022. What has improved is sentiment rather than value: by March, offers made across prime central and prime outer London were 8 per cent higher than a year earlier, and that fed into a busier summer.

Rents have moved in the opposite direction to prices for five years without interruption. Average rents in prime outer London rose 3.2 per cent in the year to July, and 1.1 per cent in prime central London. Rents in prime outer London now stand 36 per cent above their pre pandemic level, and 37 per cent above in the centre. Supply explains much of it. Rightmove data shows new rental listings across prime central and prime outer London running 14 per cent below the five year average in the first half of this year, as landlords sold out ahead of, and in response to, the Renters' Rights Act.

For the household, a market that transacts more while pricing lower is a market in motion. Owners who have watched values slide for three years are selling, letting, or holding property they no longer occupy full time. Each of those decisions produces work: closing a house, preparing one for a tenant, running a residence that is empty for months and must be ready at short notice.
articles.why: A capital where the sale price falls and the rent rises produces more moves, more lettings and more properties held in reserve. That is precisely the work an estate manager is hired to hold together.
articles.src: Knight Frank, via Property Investor Today

articles.title: The family office chief of staff acquires a published pay ladder, and it climbs with the complexity of the principal rather than the size of the house
articles.body:
A salary guide issued this year by Resonance Search, a firm that runs a dedicated chief of staff practice, sets out what the role pays in 2026 and, more usefully, what moves the number. At a single family office below USD 500 million in assets, the base sits between USD 175,000 and USD 200,000. Between USD 500 million and USD 2 billion, it runs from USD 200,000 to USD 300,000. Above USD 2 billion the base starts at USD 300,000, and where the chief of staff functions as the second most senior person in the office, with broad authority and direct access to the principal, cash compensation above USD 1 million is described as not uncommon.

The determinants are worth reading closely, because they are the same ones that govern senior household pay. Scope comes first: a chief of staff confined to personal logistics and household management is paid less than one who spans investment operations, family governance and philanthropy, and roles that cover both sit at the top of the range. Location adds 15 to 25 per cent in New York and San Francisco, where family offices bid for the same operators as private equity firms and hedge funds. The reporting line matters too. Those who report directly to the principal are paid more than those reporting to a family office chief executive or chief operating officer.

The fourth factor is the principal. Multiple operating businesses, substantial property holdings, an active philanthropy and multi generational family dynamics create a fundamentally harder job than a single concentrated position and a simpler private life. The guide argues that compensation should reflect that difficulty, which is a polite way of saying that the same job title is worth very different sums in two houses of comparable wealth.

Bonuses are discretionary almost everywhere, typically 10 to 30 per cent of base, assessed holistically by the principal rather than by formula. Some offices attach outcome linked bonuses to specific projects: a property acquisition, a completed succession process, a major operational build out. Equity does not exist, because a family office is a private wealth vehicle rather than a company, though carried interest in particular investment vehicles is sometimes offered to long tenured hires at offices with active direct investment programmes. The trade against a corporate route is stated frankly: less upside, more stability, and a role that can last five to ten years or longer.
articles.why: This is the ceiling above a house manager's career, and the ladder is published. The skills that lift the number are scope, direct access to the principal and the ability to run operations and advisers at once.

articles.title: Heesen unveils the largest steel yacht it has ever built, and starts construction before an owner has been found
articles.body:
Heesen Yachts has revealed the 72.3 metre Project Ananda, the largest steel vessel in the Dutch yard's history and the first design released under the ownership of Laurens Last, who acquired the company last year. Exterior and interior are by Sinot Yacht Architecture and Design, with the interior built in house by Heesen Interiors. At roughly 1,750 gross tonnes, she is a significant step up in scale for a yard long associated with fast aluminium hulls.

The commercial logic is the interesting part. Ananda is being built on speculation, under what Heesen calls a Smart Custom platform: construction begins before a buyer signs, with substantial personalisation retained within a hull and general arrangement already fixed. Construction is scheduled to start in November 2026, with launch and delivery anticipated in 2030. For a market where a new commission at a leading yard can mean waiting years for a slot, an on spec build of this size is a way of selling time as much as space.

The technical specification is built around endurance and comfort rather than speed. The steel hull was tank tested at the University of Southampton's Wolfson Unit, validating resistance, trim, heave and wave response. Hybrid propulsion pairs twin MTU engines with power take in and power take off gearboxes, giving a range of 5,000 nautical miles at 12 knots. That is transoceanic capability in a yacht designed for long stays aboard rather than short coastal seasons.

The interior programme signals where owner expectations have moved. The lower deck holds a spa and beach club with a snow shower and a hyperbaric chamber, equipment that belongs to a wellness facility rather than a saloon. A yacht carrying that specification needs interior crew who can run treatment spaces, manage specialist equipment and coordinate visiting practitioners, alongside the traditional service department.
articles.why: Wellness infrastructure aboard changes the shape of the interior team, and an on spec build of this scale shortens the wait for a family that wants a large yacht without a four year commission.

articles.title: One Geneva watch sale takes USD 96.3 million, and the independent maker moves to the top of the saleroom
articles.body:
The collectible watch market has just closed the strongest eighteen months it has ever recorded. Phillips' Geneva Watch Auction: XXIII, held on 9 and 10 May in association with Bacs and Russo, realised CHF 74,846,995, or USD 96,328,083, across 225 lots. It is the highest grossing single watch auction in history. Of those 225 lots, 224 sold, a rate of 99.5 per cent. Fourteen watches passed CHF 1 million and 43 world records fell in one weekend.

The trajectory is steeper than the headline. In 2021 the benchmark for a watch sale was USD 74.5 million. That record stood until November 2025, when the same house's anniversary sale reached CHF 66.8 million, or USD 83 million. Geneva XXIII broke that six months later by USD 13 million. Phillips closed 2025 at USD 290.5 million in watch auction sales, the highest annual total any house has recorded, and USD 370 million including private sales. All five major houses reported record watch revenue that year.

The defining lots explain what collectors are paying for. A stainless steel Patek Philippe Reference 1518 from 1943 sold for CHF 14,190,000, a world record for a vintage Patek Philippe wristwatch. An F.P. Journe FFC Prototype from the collection of Francis Ford Coppola made USD 10,755,000, the first wristwatch by an independent maker to break USD 10 million. A Patek Philippe Reference 2523 world timer led Geneva XXIII at CHF 7.96 million. An Audemars Piguet Grosse Pièce pocket watch from 1921 set a house record at USD 7,736,000 in the maison's 150th year.

The structural story is the rise of the independents. F.P. Journe, Philippe Dufour and Rexhep Rexhepi now draw bidding contests once reserved for Patek Philippe and Rolex, with strong results following for Kari Voutilainen, Ferdinand Berthoud and Greubel Forsey. Collectors are paying more for low production hand finishing than for much of mass luxury. The buyer base is also younger and remote: roughly 32 per cent of Phillips buyers in 2025 were Millennial or Generation Z, and 96 per cent of its bidders participated online.
articles.why: Watches are now treated as an asset class alongside art and motor cars, which means the pieces in a principal's safe carry insurance, valuation and transport obligations. Knowing which names command that money is part of cultural fluency.

briefs.b: Knight Frank recorded 17 per cent fewer lettings deals above GBP 5,000 per week in prime central London in the first half of 2026 than in the same period of 2025, reversing a 21 per cent jump the year before. The agency attributes the hesitation to the change of government and to wealth taxes rumoured for the autumn Budget. Across London and the Home Counties, where tenants are more often British based, the fall was 4 per cent.

briefs.t: Wellness moves into the crew mess
briefs.b: Demand for specialist interior crew aboard large yachts continues to grow, covering spa therapists, nurses, hairdressers, beauticians and Pilates and yoga instructors. A spa therapist with advanced training earns from EUR 4,000 to EUR 5,500 a month on vessels above 40 metres, with a nurse on similar terms and equal rotation above 80 metres. Reformer Pilates is among the modalities owners now request by name.

Entry level butler positions pay from USD 55,000 to USD 75,000, while senior head butlers running large estates earn from USD 120,000 to more than USD 200,000, and posts carrying international travel run past USD 300,000. Live in arrangements add 20 to 40 per cent in total value once accommodation, utilities and meals are counted. Middle East markets pay 40 to 60 per cent above equivalent United States and United Kingdom rates.

briefs.t: The hybrid profile becomes the benchmark
briefs.b: Family offices are increasingly hiring people who trained in an accounting firm, investment fund or private bank before moving into private service, on the view that the combination delivers governance discipline without corporate bureaucracy. Roles in highest demand run from chief financial officers and investment directors to chiefs of staff, estate directors and assistants to principals, across London, Gibraltar, Miami, Geneva, Dubai and Monaco.

strap: A daily dispatch from the world you are entering

lead.title: Washington turns the private household into a regulated workplace, and every family with staff there will need written terms
lead.standfirst: A Domestic Worker Bill of Rights signed in March gives nannies, housekeepers and estate staff minimum wage, overtime and a written agreement from 1 July 2027, and it captures anyone paid for four hours of domestic work in a month.
lead.body:
Washington state's Domestic Worker Bill of Rights was signed into law in March 2026 and takes effect on 1 July 2027. It applies to any hiring entity that pays a person to perform domestic work in a private residence for four or more hours in a month, a threshold low enough to capture the fortnightly housekeeper as well as the full resident household team. The law does not distinguish between a family employing one cleaner and a principal running a staffed estate. Both are employers.

The obligations are the ones a company would recognise. A covered worker must be given a written agreement identifying the position and the rate of pay. Minimum wage and overtime apply. Advance notice of termination is required. The law prohibits conduct that creates an intimidating, hostile or offensive working environment, extends anti-discrimination protection to certain domestic workers and forbids retaliation against a worker who asserts these rights. Enforcement runs through complaints to the Department of Labor and Industries or through private legal action, which means a disputed dismissal in a private house can now end in a state file rather than a quiet settlement.

Washington is not inventing the direction of travel, only accelerating it. Seattle has operated a domestic workers ordinance since 2018. California's Domestic Worker Bill of Rights already extends overtime to certain personal attendants working in the home. At federal level the position has long been unambiguous: household workers are employees rather than independent contractors, they are non-exempt and therefore owed time and a half beyond forty hours in a week, and once cash wages reach USD 3,000 in 2026 the employer must withhold and pay FICA contributions of 15.3 per cent and issue a Form W-2. What changes in Washington is the paperwork, the notice and the exposure.

The operational consequence lands on whoever runs the house. Someone has to hold the written agreements, log the hours of a rota that has traditionally been elastic, record rest breaks, document a termination before it happens and keep the payroll file in a state that survives an inspection. In a single-staff household that person is often the principal's assistant. In a staffed estate it is the house or estate manager, and the role moves further away from hospitality and closer to human resources. Agencies placing staff in Washington will be asked for compliant contract templates well before the 2027 date, because the families who plan properly will want the documents in place a full season early.
lead.why: Private service is moving from private arrangement to documented employment. The professional who can produce a written agreement, an accurate hours record and a clean payroll file is the one a family keeps when the rules tighten.
lead.src: Davis Wright Tremaine, Employment, Labor and Benefits

articles.title: Family offices hold 42 per cent of the portfolio in alternatives, and six in ten intend to move the allocation again within a year
articles.body:
The UBS Global Family Office Report 2026 surveyed 307 family offices with an average family net worth of USD 2.7 billion and average assets under management of USD 1.3 billion. The average portfolio now splits roughly 41 per cent across developed market equities and fixed income, 42 per cent into alternative investments and the remainder into cash and other holdings. Private equity, venture capital and private credit together account for about 29 per cent of the average North American portfolio.

The more striking figure is intent. Sixty per cent of the offices surveyed said they plan to change their strategic asset allocation over the coming twelve months, against 35 per cent who said the same a year earlier. Among those actively making changes, real estate is being trimmed from roughly 11 per cent towards 8 per cent, and private equity from about 21 per cent towards 18 per cent. Capital that used to sit in buildings is moving into credit and into direct stakes in operating companies.

A family that owns less property as an investment does not necessarily own fewer houses. It owns them for a different reason. The residence stops being counted as part of the return and starts being counted as a cost line, which is precisely when household budgets, staffing levels and supplier contracts come under review. Estate managers who can show what a house costs to run, and what each line buys, are arguing from a stronger position than those who cannot.

The shift towards private and direct investment also has a logistical shadow. Direct deals require travel to see the asset, meetings that cannot be delegated and diaries that move at short notice. The households attached to those offices absorb that volatility: more unscheduled flights, more guests to be housed, more principals arriving home at hours that were not on the plan.
articles.why: When property is reclassified from investment to expense, the household budget is examined line by line. Knowing the true annual cost of the house, and being able to defend it, becomes part of the job.

articles.title: Dubai sells 296 homes above USD 10 million in six months, and the prime market pulls away from the rest of the city
articles.body:
Dubai's prime residential sector recorded 296 sales of homes priced above USD 10 million in the first half of 2026, worth a combined USD 5.1 billion, an increase of 14 per cent on the same period a year earlier. The second quarter alone accounted for 131 of those deals. No other city in the world currently clears that many transactions at that level in six months.

The wider market tells a calmer story. The second quarter produced roughly AED 110 billion of sales across about 38,300 transactions, a clear slowdown from the record pace of 2025, with prices rising from 5 to 7 per cent year on year and citywide gross rental yields near 6.6 per cent. Knight Frank has described the result as an increasingly two-speed market, in which prime villa communities continue to outperform while apartment-led districts normalise.

The villa is the point. Buyers at the top of this market are acquiring land, staff accommodation, garages, guest wings and pools rather than lateral apartments, and each of those purchases creates a household rather than a pied-a-terre. Palm Jumeirah, Emirates Hills, Jumeirah Bay and the Dubai Hills villa communities are now home to a permanent, year-round service population rather than a seasonal one.

For the private service market, Dubai has become the counterweight to the European season. Households there run through the summer, when maintenance is at its hardest and staff turnover is highest, and pay accordingly: the Gulf and Monaco sit at the top of international compensation tables for senior household roles. What the emirate still lacks is depth of experienced local candidates, which is why so many senior placements there are made from London, Paris and Geneva.
articles.why: Every USD 10 million villa sold is a household to be staffed, run and maintained in a climate that punishes neglect. Prime sales volume is the closest thing this market has to a hiring forecast.

articles.title: NetJets curtails sales of its jet cards, and access to an aircraft becomes something a family has to secure well in advance
articles.body:
In early August 2026 NetJets limited sales of its jet card and lease products, citing record retention rates among existing customers and surging demand from its own fractional owners. The company is not short of business. It flew 266,500 flights in the first six months of 2026, which amounts to 13.6 per cent of all business jet departures worldwide, and its departures grew 11.8 per cent over the period. Flexjet, the other large fractional operator, grew 11.0 per cent.

The backdrop is a market running well above its historic norm. The global business jet fleet stands at about 24,270 aircraft and flight activity is roughly 32 per cent above pre-pandemic levels. Demand of that order, combined with delivery backlogs at the manufacturers, means the fractional operators can now choose their customers rather than recruit them.

The jet card has been the household's flexible instrument for a decade: a block of hours bought without owning a share, used to cover the weeks when the family's own arrangement did not stretch. Withdrawing it removes the easy overflow option and pushes families back towards fractional shares, which require a longer commitment, or towards the charter market, where August pricing has been unforgiving.

Whoever books the aircraft is therefore doing a different job. It is no longer a matter of calling one provider on the morning of departure. It means holding relationships with several operators, understanding which have availability in which region, knowing the peak day rules and the callout windows inside each contract, and putting requests in earlier than the principal would naturally think to ask.
articles.why: When the flexible product disappears, the value of the person arranging travel shifts from booking to procurement: contracts, alternatives and lead times, held in advance of the request.

articles.title: Monterey sells USD 747.9 million of motor cars in three days, and the garage becomes the fastest moving asset in the house
articles.body:
Five auction houses sold USD 747.9 million of collector cars at Monterey between 13 and 15 August, according to Hagerty's tally. That is 73 per cent above the USD 432.8 million posted over the same days in 2025 and comfortably beyond the previous Monterey record of roughly USD 471 million set in 2022. Pre-sale forecasts had topped out near USD 500 million.

Volume did not drive it. Some 844 of 1,124 lots sold, a sell-through rate of 75 per cent, almost identical to last year. The average price did the work, rising 64 per cent to USD 866,107, and eleven cars made eight figures, more than the previous five Monterey weeks combined. A 1964 Shelby Cobra Daytona Coupe took USD 42,905,000 at Gooding Christie's, a record for any American car. A 2026 Ferrari Luce sold as a charity lot for USD 40 million, a 1996 McLaren F1 GTR made USD 34,655,000, a record for a British car, and a 1963 Corvette Grand Sport reached USD 18,705,000. Ferrari took seven of the ten highest results of the week.

Beneath the headline the market was selective to the point of severity. Only one of the first seventeen prewar cars offered on the Thursday hammered above its low estimate. A 1962 Aston Martin DB4 GT Zagato that made USD 14.3 million in 2015 failed to sell at a bid of USD 11,750,000. A 1936 Mercedes-Benz 500K Roadster went 54 per cent below low estimate. Singular cars with unimpeachable history were fought over. Good but ordinary examples were not.

A collection that reprices this quickly stops being decoration. Insurance schedules, agreed values, storage conditions, transport bookings and maintenance records all have to keep pace, and the person who holds those files is usually inside the household rather than at the auction house. Concours week itself is a logistical operation: enclosed transport booked months ahead, drivers, accommodation in a saturated market and a car that must arrive in a condition worth its estimate.
articles.why: Collections held in the house move in value faster than the house does. Accurate records, correct storage and competent transport are service work, and they carry seven-figure consequences.

articles.title: Singapore refines the conditions attached to family office tax incentives, and the new terms took effect this month
articles.body:
The Monetary Authority of Singapore has refined the economic conditions attached to the tax incentive schemes used by single family office funds, with the changes taking effect from 1 August 2026. The two schemes remain section 13O, the onshore fund exemption, and section 13U, the enhanced-tier exemption.

The thresholds are unchanged in shape. Section 13O requires a minimum of S$20 million in designated investments and at least two investment professionals, of whom at least one is not a family member. Section 13U requires S$50 million and three investment professionals, again with at least one from outside the family. Both carry a capital deployment requirement of the lower of S$10 million or 10 per cent of assets under management into eligible local investments. The refinements raise the assets under management thresholds attached to the higher local business spending tiers and tighten the minimum local spending expected of larger funds, while giving offices more operational flexibility elsewhere.

The scale of what is being regulated is easy to underestimate. More than 2,000 single family offices held these incentives at the end of December 2025, a figure that has grown steadily through the decade and made Singapore the principal Asian base for internationally mobile family capital.

The household follows the office. A family that anchors its structure in Singapore places people there: a principal residence, school places, drivers, a house manager who can operate across time zones and a travel pattern that runs through Hong Kong, Tokyo, Sydney and the Gulf rather than through Europe. Employment terms, work passes and domestic helper regulations in Singapore are precise, and staff are expected to be documented correctly from the first day.
articles.why: Where a family puts its structure determines where it puts its house, and therefore where the jobs are. Reading jurisdiction news is how a candidate anticipates the market rather than following it.

briefs.t: The nanny tax threshold rises to USD 3,000
briefs.b: Cash wages of USD 3,000 or more paid to a household employee during 2026 trigger FICA obligations of 15.3 per cent of wages, up from USD 2,800 in 2025. Any employee paid at or above that level, or from whom federal income tax was withheld, must receive a Form W-2. The threshold now catches part-time and seasonal household staff in most markets.

briefs.t: Private jet departures return to growth
briefs.b: Global business jet departures reached about 78,074 in the first full week of August, the first year on year increase recorded in three weeks. Fractional and charter volumes were broadly flat on the previous week, with growth concentrated in Florida, California and Texas.

briefs.t: 165,000 millionaires expected to move this year
briefs.b: The 2026 edition of the Henley Private Wealth Migration Report projects roughly 165,000 high net worth individuals relocating internationally this year, up from about 142,000 in 2025. That is more than 600 people changing country on every working day, each one a household to be closed, moved or opened.

briefs.t: The estate manager average sits near USD 152,000
briefs.b: Compensation survey data for estate and household roles puts the United States average for an estate manager, including base salary and bonus, at about USD 151,830, with the 75th percentile near USD 181,179. Packages in California and New York run materially above the national figure, and senior multi-property roles in the Gulf and Monaco higher still.
briefs.src: Talent Gurus household staff compensation guide
