lead.title: California puts a one-time levy on 200 fortunes to a public vote, and the households attached to them start reading the calendar
lead.standfirst: A union backed initiative taxing billionaire net worth at 5 per cent has qualified for the November ballot, and the private staff who run Californian houses are already inside the consequences.
lead.body:
The measure known as the Billionaire Tax Act qualified for California's November 2026 ballot on 17 June, after proponents submitted well over 1.5 million signatures against the 875,000 valid signatures the state requires. It proposes a one-time levy of 5 per cent on the net worth of California billionaires, a group generally estimated at around 200 people, with proceeds directed to health care, education and food assistance programmes. Supporters put the potential yield at figures approaching USD 100 billion.

The number is not the interesting part. The mechanism is. A wealth levy is assessed against residency at a fixed moment, which means the question it poses to a household is not how much but where, and on which date. Analysts at the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy have modelled revenue and constitutional exposure alike, and opponents have already filed two counter initiatives, one requiring pre-election audits of programmes funded by special tax measures and another seeking to shield personal savings accounts from taxation. Governor Gavin Newsom has said publicly that he expects the measure to be defeated.

What matters for private service is that the whole debate now runs through the domestic calendar. Californian residency is not settled by a change of address. It is settled by domicile, by day counts, by where the family's life is visibly centred, and by a documentary trail that includes travel records, card statements and, in disputed cases, device location. The state has some of the most active residency audit practice in the country, and the year of a move is where disputes concentrate.

That trail is generated almost entirely by the household. The house diary, the flight manifests, the standing orders to suppliers, the school run, the vehicle registrations, the club memberships and the staff rotas are the record of where a family actually lives. A principal may believe the family left in March. The evidence of March is held by whoever ran the house that month.

California is not an isolated case. At least a dozen states have advanced measures aimed at the top of the wealth distribution this year, and the pattern is consistent: the assessment date is fixed, and the burden of proving absence falls on the taxpayer. The private houses of Los Angeles, Malibu, Montecito and Atherton employ a great many people, and the future of those posts will be decided in part by a vote in November.
lead.why: When a principal's tax position turns on residence, the household record becomes evidence. Accurate diaries, clean itineraries and disciplined record keeping are no longer administrative housekeeping, they are part of the family's legal position.

articles.title: A move only counts if it survives an audit, and the people who prove it work in the house
articles.body:
The rule most often quoted is the 183 day threshold: spend more than half a year in a state with an income tax and you may be treated as resident there regardless of where you say you live. In practice the threshold is only the crudest of the tests. States apply a facts and circumstances assessment of domicile, asking where the permanent home really is, where the family's life is centred, where the valuable possessions sit and where the business and financial ties remain.

The evidence assembled in a contested case is domestic in nature. Auditors review travel logs, credit card records and, increasingly, mobile phone location data to establish where a person actually spent their days. Retaining a property in the former state, keeping a car registered there, maintaining club memberships or leaving significant staff in place all count against a claim to have left. The transition year, when ties overlap and timing matters most, is where residency disputes cluster.

None of this is theoretical for a house manager. The staff rota is a record of occupancy. The provisioning orders show when a kitchen was running. The maintenance log shows when a pool was opened. A household that keeps a precise, contemporaneous record of the principal's presence is producing, without intending to, the strongest evidence available in a residency review. A household that keeps a vague one is producing the opposite.

The practical discipline is simple and rarely taught. Record arrivals and departures rather than reconstructing them later. Keep the house diary consistent with the flight record. Note when a property was closed and when it was reopened. Where a family holds houses in several jurisdictions, treat each as a separate ledger rather than a single blurred year. The advisers will ask for all of it eventually, and they will ask the person who was there.
articles.why: Private service is increasingly a documentary craft. The value of a well kept house diary is no longer only operational, it is evidential, and the professional who understands that is materially more useful to the family office.

articles.title: The family office runs at USD 3 million a year, and 86 per cent of them have no plan for who takes over
articles.body:
J.P. Morgan Private Bank's 2026 Global Family Office Report surveyed 333 family offices worldwide with an average net worth of USD 1.6 billion. Two thirds named geopolitics as the leading risk they face. More striking, for anyone working inside these structures, is what the survey found about the offices themselves: 86 per cent said they lacked a clear succession plan for key decision makers, and 53 per cent of business owning families identified succession as a top concern.

The cost base is rising with the complexity. The average family office now runs at roughly USD 3 million a year, climbing to USD 6.6 million for offices with more than USD 1 billion in assets. Around 11 per cent of those surveyed spent more than USD 7 million, with over a quarter of that expenditure going to outsourced services such as legal work, trading and cybersecurity. The report attributes the increase directly to competition for talent and the need for specialised skills, alongside a shift towards hiring non family professionals.

The shortage has a demographic explanation. As the baby boom generation retires from these roles, there are fewer Generation X professionals with the requisite experience behind them, and the millennial cohort is only now reaching the prime of its career. Practitioners describe a great deal of demand meeting very little supply. In large offices, staff turnover has been measured at roughly one departure every nine months.

For the household side of the structure, the implication is favourable and demanding in equal measure. Favourable, because the market is paying for competence and hiring outside the family to get it. Demanding, because the professional who arrives into an office with no succession plan and a rising outsourcing bill is joining an organisation that has not yet decided how it will be run in five years. The people who thrive in that setting are the ones who can document a process, hand it over cleanly and make themselves legible to whoever comes next.
articles.why: A house does not sit outside the family office, it reports into it. Understanding how that office is staffed, what it costs and where its gaps lie is the difference between being an employee of the family and being a professional within its structure.

articles.title: Business jet backlogs rise nearly 20 per cent in the second quarter, and the wait for a new aeroplane gets longer again
articles.body:
Global Jet Capital's latest quarterly assessment of the business aviation market, reported on 18 August, describes a sector that is stable in transaction terms but carrying an order book that keeps expanding. Manufacturer backlogs jumped by close to 20 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, and lead times are lengthening accordingly.

The delivery figures behind that backlog have been strong. GAMA recorded 854 business jet shipments in 2025, an increase of 11.8 per cent on the previous year, with total airplane billings of USD 31.0 billion, up 16.1 per cent. Through the first quarter of 2026, business jet deliveries rose a further 14.9 per cent to 162 units, and the value of airplane deliveries reached USD 6.1 billion, 19.1 per cent above the same period a year earlier. The association's second quarter report is scheduled for release this week.

A growing backlog against rising deliveries means the same thing it means in any manufacturing sector: demand is being placed faster than it can be filled. For the large cabin aircraft that matter most to internationally mobile families, that translates into delivery slots measured in years rather than months, and into a secondary market where a good aircraft available now carries a premium over one available in 2029.

The operational consequence sits with whoever coordinates the family's movement. When new capacity is scarce, existing aircraft fly more, maintenance windows become harder to schedule, and the gap between what the aircraft can do and what the calendar demands is filled by charter, by fractional programmes or by commercial flights that nobody wants to book. Planning a season around an aircraft that is fully committed is a different discipline from planning around one with slack in it.
articles.why: The private aircraft is the single most constrained asset in most households' logistics. Knowing that lead times are lengthening changes how far ahead a season should be planned and how early alternative lift should be secured.

articles.title: Italy leads the fine wine recovery, and nine Tuscan labels now account for four fifths of the region's trade
articles.body:
Liv-ex, the benchmark exchange for the secondary fine wine market, shows a recovery that is modest but broad. The Liv-ex 100, the platform's flagship index, gained 0.4 per cent over the first seven months of 2026, set against a stronger 3.3 per cent rise over the past twelve months. The Liv-ex 1000, the widest measure, is broadly flat in 2026 at 0.3 per cent and trails at 1.2 per cent over the year.

The leadership has changed hands. The Italy 100 has risen 1.5 per cent since the start of the year and 2.9 per cent over twelve months, ahead of the Champagne 50 at 1.6 and 2.6 per cent, and well ahead of the Burgundy 150 at 0.8 and 1.9 per cent. The Liv-ex Bordeaux 500 remains negative on both measures, at minus 0.3 per cent for the year to date and minus 0.4 per cent over twelve months. The best performing individual labels of 2026 alternate between Piedmont and Tuscany, led by Giacomo Conterno's Barolo Monfortino Riserva 2005 at 25.2 per cent, Soldera Case Basse's Sangiovese Toscana 2020 at 20.5 per cent and Frescobaldi's Masseto 2016 at 18.7 per cent.

Liv-ex attributes Italy's resilience specifically to Tuscany. Piedmont wines, generally rarer and more expensive, have seen sharper declines, while Tuscan labels have held their prices on solid trading volume. The concentration is remarkable. Of 157 Tuscan wines traded so far this year across multiple vintages, just nine account for more than 80 per cent of the region's traded value: Sassicaia, Tignanello, Ornellaia, Masseto, Guado al Tasso, Biondi-Santi Brunello di Montalcino, Solaia, Fuligni Brunello di Montalcino and Soldera Case Basse. A year earlier it took 21 wines out of 282 to reach the same share.

A private cellar is an asset with a market price, an insurance value and a service life. Knowing which regions are holding value, which are drifting and how narrow the liquid part of a market has become is not connoisseurship for its own sake. It is the difference between a cellar that is managed and one that is merely stored.
articles.why: Whoever holds the cellar keys is holding a priced asset. Reading the indices, understanding concentration and knowing what is genuinely tradeable are part of the cultural fluency a senior house appointment now assumes.

briefs.t: The second home in the frame
briefs.b: New York's governor and the mayor of New York City are advancing a proposed annual surcharge on high value second homes, commonly described as a pied a terre tax. The proposal focuses on properties valued above USD 5 million that are not primary residences. Its path runs through the state legislative and budget cycles.

briefs.t: A record year for the jet
briefs.b: GAMA recorded 854 business jet deliveries in 2025, up 11.8 per cent, with airplane billings of USD 31.0 billion, up 16.1 per cent. Business jet shipments rose a further 14.9 per cent to 162 units in the first quarter of 2026. The association's second quarter report is due this week.

briefs.t: The Gulf hedges, it does not leave
briefs.b: Henley & Partners recorded a 41 per cent rise in enquiries from UAE based individuals between the fourth quarter of 2025 and the first quarter of 2026, with applications for alternative residence or citizenship up 29 per cent. The firm characterises the movement as contingency planning by families using the Emirates as a base, not an exodus from it.

Callan Family Office reached USD 10 billion in assets under management this year, four years after being founded. Elsewhere in the sector, the multi family office Pathstone has said it plans to hire more than 40 new employees this year, citing demand for outsourced trust, tax and accounting work.

lead.title: Two in five family offices report a cyber attack, and the household is increasingly where the intruder gets in
lead.standfirst: Deloitte finds that 43 per cent of family offices have been attacked within the past two years, and that the weakest point is rarely the investment desk.
lead.body:
Deloitte Private's family office cybersecurity research puts a number on something the private world has preferred to discuss in the abstract. Some 43 per cent of family offices surveyed reported at least one cyber attack in the preceding 12 to 24 months, and a quarter of those affected reported three or more. The exposure rises with size and with geography: 57 per cent of North American offices reported an attack, against 41 per cent in Europe and 24 per cent in Asia Pacific, and among offices managing more than USD 1 billion the figure reaches 62 per cent.

The methods are unglamorous. Phishing was involved in 93 per cent of reported incidents, malware in 35 per cent and social engineering in 23 per cent. These are not exotic intrusions into trading systems. They are messages that look like a supplier, a bank, a lawyer or a principal, and they succeed because someone in the structure has the authority to move money and the habit of moving it quickly. Business email compromise, invoice manipulation and payment redirection remain the most productive financial attacks against private structures, and they land on precisely the people who approve household expenditure.

The preparedness gap is the more striking finding. Roughly 31 per cent of family offices have no cyber incident response plan at all. An organisation that will spend months on the due diligence of a single co-investment will often have no written answer to the question of who is telephoned, in what order, on the morning a payment is discovered to have gone to the wrong account.

The household sits inside this perimeter and is rarely counted as part of it. Domestic staff hold alarm codes, guest lists, delivery schedules, medical appointments, school runs and the wireless credentials of the house. Estate managers hold vendor lists and approve invoices. Travel coordinators hold itineraries. Very little of that information is protected by anything more than the discretion of the person holding it, and much of it is transacted on personal devices, in messaging applications, outside any system the family office controls. A single compromised household telephone can yield a family's movements for the next three months.

That is where the risk stops being financial. Movement data, vessel positions, aircraft records and school routines convert a data breach into a physical one. The practical response is not technical sophistication so much as ordinary discipline: verification of payment instructions by a second channel and a known voice, separate devices or accounts for household business, restraint in group messaging, and a written escalation route that every member of staff has read. Synthetic voice and video have made the instruction that sounds exactly like the principal an unreliable form of authority.
lead.why: Whoever runs the house is part of the family's security architecture whether or not anyone has said so. Verifying a payment instruction, keeping itineraries off open channels and knowing who to call first are now core competences of private service, not IT department concerns.
lead.src: Deloitte Private, The Family Office Cybersecurity Report

articles.title: Aspen dollar sales fall 51 per cent in the first half, and the quietest mountain season since 2020 is not a distressed one
articles.body:
Between 1 January and 30 June 2026, combined dollar sales across Aspen and Snowmass fell 51 per cent against the same period a year earlier, with unit sales down 39 per cent, according to figures compiled by the Estin Report and published locally. Aspen alone recorded a fall of 56 per cent in dollar volume and 44 per cent in transactions. It is the slowest first half the valley has seen since the pandemic years of 2020 and 2021.

The contraction is sharpest precisely where the private service market lives. Sales above USD 10 million fell 56 per cent by value and 48 per cent by number of transactions. At the very top, deals above USD 20 million dropped from 19 in the first half of 2025 to 13 in the first half of 2026, a fall of about a third.

What makes the numbers unusual is the context. Equity markets have been at record levels through much of the period, and the wealth that buys in Aspen has not disappeared. Local analysts describe the market as high value but quiet rather than distressed. Prices have held. What has thinned is supply and the willingness of existing owners to sell, and a market with almost nothing available records very few transactions regardless of how much demand exists.

For households, a market that stops trading behaves differently from one that is falling. Families keep houses longer, which lengthens the horizon of the people who run them. Renovation cycles replace acquisition cycles, and the estate manager's year fills with contractors, permits and phased works rather than handovers and inventories. Continuity of staff becomes more valuable to the principal, because the person who knows the building becomes the only continuous record of it.
articles.why: A market that trades rarely rewards long service. Where houses change hands slowly, the household team becomes the institutional memory of the property, and renovation management moves to the centre of the estate manager's role.
articles.src: The Aspen Times, citing the Estin Report

articles.title: The Mediterranean charter season runs as much as 30 per cent behind last year, and August weeks are still being discounted
articles.body:
For several seasons the standard advice in the charter market was that the best hulls were committed by early spring and that a family deciding in June would be choosing from what nobody else wanted. That advice did not hold in 2026. Summer charters in the Mediterranean have run between 20 and 30 per cent below last year, and a significant number of yachts have carried discounts and incentives into the last weeks of July and August.

Jonathan Beckett, chief executive of the brokerage Burgess, told CNBC that American bookings for the Mediterranean began the year strongly and then slowed following the outbreak of conflict involving Iran, and estimated that the summer charter season may finish about 30 per cent down. Premium vessels remained available at the start of July, some with upgrades or flexible terms attached, a situation the market had not seen since the years immediately after the pandemic.

Demand has not vanished so much as compressed and moved later. Brokers report that the overwhelming majority of forward summer bookings still fall between June and August, but that they are being confirmed far closer to departure than they were. A yacht that once knew its season in March now learns much of it in weeks.

That compression is felt by crew before it is felt by owners. Rosters, provisioning, berth reservations and shore arrangements all depend on a calendar that is now being written at short notice, and the ability to mobilise a full guest programme in days rather than months has become the operational test of a charter operation. For the household side, the same principle applies on land: the villa, the cars, the staff and the shore programme are increasingly booked into the same narrowing window.
articles.why: Shorter lead times move the burden onto whoever executes. The estate manager or chief of staff who can assemble a full itinerary, crew, cars and shore arrangements in a fortnight is now doing what used to be a season's planning.

articles.title: Swiss watch exports rise 9.6 per cent in July, and more than a quarter of everything shipped now goes to the United States
articles.body:
Swiss watch exports reached CHF 2.63 billion in July, a rise of 9.6 per cent against July 2025, according to the Federation of the Swiss Watch Industry. The month was strong enough to pull the cumulative figure for the first seven months of the year back into positive territory, up 0.9 per cent, after a first half that had been broadly flat.

The United States did most of the work. American imports of Swiss watches rose 26.5 per cent in the month to CHF 701.3 million, which is 26.7 per cent of everything Switzerland shipped in July. The European Union rose 12.4 per cent, led by Germany, and the United Kingdom rose 9.5 per cent. Asia told the opposite story: Hong Kong was almost flat at 0.5 per cent, Singapore rose 2.3 per cent, Japan fell 3.7 per cent and mainland China fell 18.5 per cent. The United Arab Emirates fell 3.7 per cent.

The materials data shows where the growth is. Watches in precious metals rose 3.7 per cent by value, steel rose 9 per cent, and bimetallic gold and steel models rose 23.8 per cent, the strongest category of the month. Volumes rose too, with roughly 97,000 more watches shipped than in July 2025, taking total wristwatch exports to about 1.5 million units.

The geographic shift matters more than the headline. A market in which one country absorbs more than a quarter of Swiss production, while China contracts sharply, changes where the important collections are being assembled and where the specialist service, insurance and valuation infrastructure follows. For anyone who will be responsible for a principal's collection, that is not trivia. Watches are among the few high-value objects that leave the safe daily, travel in hand luggage, are worn at dinner and are lent, gifted and inherited, and the person who manages the household is usually the one who knows where each piece is.
articles.why: Cultural fluency is part of the job. Knowing what a piece is, what it is worth, how it should be serviced, insured and transported, and how to discuss it without valuing it aloud, is ordinary competence in a senior private household.
articles.src: Federation of the Swiss Watch Industry, reported by WWD

articles.title: Wealthy collectors now hold a fifth of their wealth in art, and the collection stops being decoration on the balance sheet
articles.body:
The Art Basel and UBS survey of global collecting, compiled by Arts Economics from responses of some 3,100 high net worth individuals across ten markets, found that collectors allocated an average of 20 per cent of their wealth to art, up from 15 per cent a year earlier. Among those with more than USD 50 million in assets the figure reaches 28 per cent. Intentions point the same way: 40 per cent said they planned to buy more art over the following twelve months, while selling intentions eased to 25 per cent.

The wider market has stabilised beneath those numbers. Global art sales rose 4 per cent to an estimated USD 59.6 billion in 2025, with the dealer sector up 2 per cent at USD 34.8 billion and public auction sales up 9 per cent at USD 20.7 billion. Sentiment among dealers entering 2026 improved, with 43 per cent expecting sales to rise and 38 per cent expecting them to hold steady.

A collection at a quarter of a family's wealth is no longer furniture. It is an asset class kept in the places where the family lives, and that has consequences the balance sheet does not show. Light levels, humidity, hanging, insurance schedules, condition reports, loan agreements with museums, transport, customs paperwork and the logistics of moving works between residences all sit somewhere in the household's operating rhythm.

The survey also found that 96 per cent of respondents intend to attend art events during 2026, and 48 per cent expect to attend more than the year before. Fairs, previews, openings and private views generate their own operational load: travel that must be arranged around a fixed calendar, invitations that must be tracked, and a diary that is set by the art world's year rather than the family's.
articles.why: Where a fifth of the family's wealth hangs on the walls, the household is the custodian of an asset portfolio. Condition, climate, movement records and insurance documentation become part of house management, not an outside specialism.
articles.src: The Art Basel and UBS reports, by Arts Economics

articles.title: A five villa estate opens on Crete, and the private rental continues to move away from the hotel
articles.body:
Tierras Villas opens on Crete this month, a small estate of five villas designed by Manos Kipritidis in stone and wood, each with its own pool and terraces facing the sea. The scale is the point. Five keys is not a hotel, and the property is built around the assumption that guests want a house with service rather than a room with a lobby.

The pattern is now consistent across the Greek islands and the wider Mediterranean. New openings at the top of the market are villa led, low in key count and high in staff ratio, and the guest expects a level of personal attention that resembles a private household more than it resembles hospitality. Service is delivered by people who learn a family's preferences over a week rather than a shift.

For a student of private service, this end of the market is the closest commercial analogue to the work itself. The disciplines are the same: reading a household's rhythm, anticipating rather than responding, holding a standard without being visible, and running a small team in a building that is somebody's home for the duration of their stay.
articles.why: Villa led properties recruit and train in exactly the competences a private household requires, and a season in one is among the more direct routes into estate work.

briefs.b: Palm Beach closed its 2025 to 2026 season with record sales at record prices. The median single family sale on the island reached USD 12.9 million, with average values near USD 9.8 million and still rising into 2026. The year's highest recorded transaction, a waterfront estate on Old Harbour Road, closed at USD 97.5 million.

Under the Employment Rights Act 2025, the qualifying period for ordinary unfair dismissal protection falls from two years to six months on 1 January 2027. Private households employing staff directly are covered in the same way as any other employer, which shortens considerably the window in which a placement can be ended without full process.

Singapore has passed 1,500 registered single family offices in 2026, having counted fewer than 200 seven years ago. Each new office brings with it residences, travel patterns and household staffing requirements, and the city remains one of the fastest growing private employment markets in Asia.

Housekeepers, private chefs, nannies and estate managers remain the four most requested roles across the United States, according to the Morgan & Mallet household staff industry report for 2026. Estate managers are the hardest of the four to fill, because the combination of security awareness, technical literacy and team management the role now demands is rarely found in one candidate.
