lead.title: The 75th Pebble Beach Concours closes Monterey week, and the collector's centre of gravity moves towards cars built in his own lifetime
lead.standfirst: Five auction houses, a forecast approaching half a billion dollars and a quiet generational shift in what the wealthiest households now choose to collect.
lead.body:
Every August the Monterey Peninsula becomes the centre of the collector car world. Five major auction houses, Bonhams, Broad Arrow, Gooding Christie's, Mecum and RM Sotheby's, set up within a few miles of one another, and the week closes on the links at Pebble Beach with the Concours d'Elegance, which reached its 75th edition this year. Ahead of the week, analysts at Hagerty placed the midpoint of their sales forecast at roughly USD 470 million, with an optimistic scenario near USD 496 million. Either figure would put 2026 at or beyond the existing record of USD 471.2 million, set in 2022.

What matters more than the headline number is what produced it. Lot counts were expected to stay roughly flat, and the share of reserve lots to tick up only slightly. The change was in the mix. More seven and eight figure cars were consigned this year than at any previous Monterey, and a record 177 lots were forecast to sell above USD 1 million, against a previous high of 158 in 2022. Headline consignments included a Ferrari 250 P, a McLaren F1 GTR, several Ferrari Enzos, a Chevrolet Corvette Grand Sport and a Shelby Cobra Daytona Coupe, the last two absent from the auction block since 2009.

The generational point is the interesting one. Modern supercars, meaning cars built from the mid 1980s onwards, were projected to account for roughly 60 per cent of total sales. The average model year of cars on offer has moved from 1967 to 1974 in only three years. The prewar classics and Enzo-era Ferraris that once defined the top of the Monterey leaderboard are ceding ground to machines the buyer remembers from his own youth. Taste is following demographics, and it is doing so quickly.

The market underneath these results is not uniformly strong. Hagerty's broader Market Rating, a gauge of overall collector car health, has sat around 59.01 for close to a year, squarely in flat territory, while its longer-running Market Index is down 17 per cent from its December 2022 peak. Cars valued below roughly USD 250,000 have softened noticeably. The pattern industry watchers describe is K-shaped: trophy assets keep setting records while the broad middle treads water. For context, 2025 finished at USD 432.8 million, the second-highest total on record, but strip out a single USD 26 million charity Ferrari Daytona SP3 and the growth over 2024 was a modest 4 per cent.

Sell-through rate is the number the trade watches rather than the total. Last year roughly three quarters of lots found buyers across the major houses, with wide variation between them. A high proportion of cars failing to meet reserve, even alongside record headline sales, would indicate strain inside the luxury tier itself.
lead.why: A collection of this scale is an operational responsibility before it is an aesthetic one, and the household is what moves it, insures it, stores it and enters it. Knowing which era a principal collects, and why, is the difference between administering a garage and understanding a passion.
lead.src: Modern Car Collector, via Yahoo Finance

articles.title: Discretion stops being a virtue and becomes a line in the contract, worth 15 to 20 per cent on top of the salary
articles.body: The Morgan & Mallet Beyond the Butler 2025/26 report, examined by Spear's, records something the trade has long understood but rarely priced: confidentiality now carries a measurable premium. Roles carrying strict confidentiality obligations pay 15 to 20 per cent more than comparable positions without them. In Los Angeles, 77 per cent of personal assistant roles require a non-disclosure agreement. Some households impose a social media ban outright, and others ask staff to hand in their telephones on arrival. The lengths principals will go to are instructive. One Manhattan billionaire hired a butler who had never worked on the East Coast, specifically to avoid the overlapping social circles through which household detail travels. Certain very senior placements are conducted under such secrecy that the recruiter never learns the client's identity. The premium is not paid for silence in the abstract. It is paid for the absence of any route by which information could leave the house. The pay scales attached to this are no longer domestic in scale. The United States pays the most for 60 per cent of all household roles. Private chefs reach USD 300,000, executive assistants run from USD 120,000 to USD 250,000, and at the top of the household the chief of staff reaches USD 300,000 with the estate manager at USD 250,000. American principals expect round-the-clock support and staff who can hold both private and business responsibilities, which narrows the eligible pool considerably. There is a structural reason discretion has become expensive. Families are buying more properties in more countries, and each house adds people who see things. Average tenure across household roles now sits at about three years, and nannies typically stay two to three. Shorter tenures mean more former employees carrying more knowledge, which raises the value of the ones who can be trusted not to use it.
articles.why: Discretion is the one competency that cannot be demonstrated in an interview and cannot be recovered once lost. It is now written into the contract and reflected in the number, which means it will be assessed as rigorously as any technical skill.
articles.src: Spear's, on the Morgan & Mallet Beyond the Butler 2025/26 report

articles.title: Global wealth grows 10.8 per cent in a year, and the fastest expansion happens in the band that actually employs household staff
articles.body:
UBS published the 17th edition of its Global Wealth Report on 30 June, covering 56 markets that together hold more than 92 per cent of the world's wealth. Global personal wealth rose 10.8 per cent in USD terms during 2025, the fastest pace since 2017 and well ahead of the 4.6 per cent recorded in 2024. Growth was strongest in Europe, the Middle East and Africa at 17.5 per cent, followed by the Americas at 8.5 per cent and Asia-Pacific at 5.9 per cent. Currency movements, principally the weaker dollar, amplified gains outside the United States.

The number of USD millionaires rose 1.5 per cent, close to one million new millionaires, or more than 2,600 a day. The United States accounted for almost half of them, adding over 440,000. Switzerland remains the highest-ranked market for average wealth per adult at USD 910,382, ahead of the United States and Luxembourg. More than half of all global personal wealth still sits in the United States and mainland China combined.

The segment worth watching for anyone in private service is not the millionaire count but the tier above it. UBS records that growth was particularly strong in the bands from USD 5 million to USD 100 million, the group the report calls the bigger siblings of the everyday millionaire, and that this acceleration was most pronounced in mainland China, Australia and the United States. That band is precisely where a household stops being run by the family and starts being run by staff.

UBS also flags a divergence that complicates the headline. Since 2020, average wealth and median wealth have moved apart, and the report's own tables show the gap plainly: the United States ranks second on average wealth per adult at USD 696,277, yet its median sits at USD 68,998. Residential property remains the dominant asset for most households up to the everyday millionaire level, which limits participation in market-driven gains. Future outcomes, UBS concludes, will depend increasingly on access to investable assets and the ability to diversify.
articles.why: The USD 5 million to USD 100 million band is the growth engine of private staffing demand, and it behaves differently from the billionaire tier. These are first-generation employers who often have no household template, and who rely heavily on the professionalism of the first person they hire.

articles.title: The Hamptons runs out of houses, inventory falls to 1,166 and the summer season becomes a contest for what little exists
articles.body:
The East End's second quarter, analysed by Jonathan Miller of Miller Samuel, tells a story of demand meeting an empty shelf. There were 425 sales in the quarter, 12.3 per cent below the decade average, and sales have now fallen year on year for three consecutive quarters. Inventory dropped 9.5 per cent annually to 1,166 listings, 15.8 per cent below the ten-year average, with listings down in three of the past four quarters.

Prices moved in the opposite direction. The middle of the market, from USD 1 million to USD 5 million, took a record 67.8 per cent share of total sales, with median price rising 16.1 per cent annually to USD 2.2 million. Sales below USD 1 million fell to 14.6 per cent, close to a record low, while sales at USD 5 million and above reached a high of 17.9 per cent. Miller attributes much of this to a shift in the housing stock rather than pure price growth: builders on the East End are not putting up small houses, and the modest cottages that remain are being replaced by homes two or three times their size.

The top of the market behaved as it usually does. Bridgehampton, taken with Water Mill and Sagaponack, recorded the highest median at USD 5.33 million, up 12.2 per cent year on year, and took three of the seven sales above USD 20 million in the quarter. Amagansett saw sales fall 45 per cent and volume fall 16.4 per cent, yet still posted the second-highest median at close to USD 4.3 million. Hampton Bays remains the only submarket with a median below USD 1 million, and local agents expect that to change.

Judi Desiderio of William Raveis described a winter that was slow for both sales and rentals, followed by a second quarter in which activity built like a snowball. The pattern of the past several years holds: fewer trades each year, less inventory each year, and prices that keep climbing regardless.
articles.why: Scarce inventory means families hold houses longer and renovate rather than move, which lengthens the estate manager's horizon and shifts the role from transition management towards long-term stewardship of a single property.
articles.src: 27east, on Miller Samuel and William Raveis second quarter data

articles.title: The aircraft the wealthiest actually want is a single-engine turboprop with a two-year waiting list, and it is winning on ground time
articles.body:
The Pilatus PC-12 is not a jet. It is a Swiss-built single-engine turboprop, first unveiled in 1994, and it has become one of the most sought-after aircraft in private aviation. Some 2,200 have been delivered and they have flown more than 11 million hours. Pilatus now runs a two-year waiting list for new aircraft, and brokers report pre-owned examples selling for more than they cost new. Aircraft that fetched USD 6.4 million a few years ago now trade above USD 7 million, and rarely sit on the market for more than three months. The latest version, the PC-12 PRO, starts at USD 7.8 million.

The appeal is not speed or cabin size. It is the combination of a 290 knot cruise at up to 30,000 feet, a range of 2,070 miles, and the ability to use small airfields and grass strips that jets cannot. Jonathan Clough of Jetfly, whose firm owns, manages or operates 30 PC-12s, gives the arithmetic for a run from Surrey to Saint Tropez: by jet it is 45 minutes to Farnborough, 90 minutes in the air to Toulon-Hyeres and often 90 minutes by road, at least four hours end to end. By PC-12, it is 15 minutes to Fairoaks near Woking, two hours to La Mole, and 25 minutes to Saint Tropez, three hours in total. Handling fees at Farnborough run to GBP 1,500, and double at weekends. At Fairoaks and La Mole they are in the hundreds.

The cargo door is a quiet part of the appeal. Art collectors use the aircraft to move large works that no small jet can accommodate, and Jetfly cites one client who bought a PC-12 specifically because the door took his son's full-size powered wheelchair. James Banham of Oriens Aviation notes that the aircraft held around 80 per cent of its value after ten years before the pandemic, and rather more since.

The flight data supports the anecdote. WingX recorded roughly 333,500 PC-12 flights in the first half of 2026, up 4.3 per cent year on year. Commercial operators running private charter, air taxi and air ambulance work accounted for 41 per cent of flights and grew 7.5 per cent. Fractional operators took 8 per cent and grew 6.2 per cent. North America dominates with 72.8 per cent of flights, Europe holds 12.1 per cent. Charles Robinson of Enterjet reports a 46.3 per cent rise in PC-12 charter requests year on year, driven particularly by technology founders under 35. Around 100 aircraft will be built in 2026, against 84 of the predecessor NGX delivered in 2025.
articles.why: Door-to-door time, not aircraft category, is what the principal experiences. Whoever builds the itinerary should know which small airfields exist near the destination house, because the right strip can remove an hour of road from every trip.

articles.title: The five-star hotel discovers that the surest way to fill itself is to put a hundred years of Italian coachwork on the lawn
articles.body:
Luxury hotels have always parked something desirable by the door. What has changed is that several are now staging the events themselves. In Piazza della Repubblica, the Anantara Palazzo Naiadi hosted the inaugural Anantara Concorso Roma, gathering 66 exceptionally scarce Italian cars, a field valued at around GBP 350 million, and moving them under police escort down the Via Nazionale to the parkland of Villa Borghese. It was the first concours held in Rome since 1960, and it marked a century since the 1926 Concorso Romano delle Carrozzerie.

The programme ran three days: a rooftop reception for entrants and sponsors the night before, a black-tie gala in the Palazzo Brancaccio, and judging that awarded Best in Show to a one-off 16-cylinder 1932 Maserati V4 Sport Zagato, once owned by the personal physician of Pope Pius XII, returning to Rome for the first time in 90 years. Its owner, the retired New York fund manager Lawrence Auriana, keeps around 100 cars in Connecticut and flies a handful to events of this kind. What distinguishes the Rome event is its restriction to a single nationality of construction, across 16 classes. A second edition is confirmed for 1 to 4 April 2027.

The model has precedent. Lake Como's Villa d'Este held its first concours in 1929 and, after BMW's sponsorship at the turn of the millennium, has become the event by which the others are judged, fielding over 50 cars each May. Sir Michael Kadoorie, owner of The Peninsula Hotels, competes there and at Pebble Beach, and his Carmel property, The Quail, hosts what has arguably become the more culturally current gathering. This year's 6,000 all-inclusive Quail tickets sold out at GBP 1,170 a head, alongside six-figure commercial stands. The Peninsula Classics Best of the Best, invitation only since 2015, draws the Best in Show winners from Pebble Beach, Villa d'Este, The Quail, Amelia Island, Salon Prive, Hampton Court, Goodwood's Cartier Style et Luxe and the Palm Beach Cavallino Classic.

The economics are candid. William Heinecke, owner of Anantara's parent Minor Hotels, told Spear's he is not sure the return is quantifiable, given the scale of the investment, but that the event provides an experience and, not incidentally, introduces the brand to American collectors in a market where Anantara has no property. Owners cover transport: around GBP 8,000 to ship a car door to door from Los Angeles to Rome, or GBP 15,000 to GBP 18,000 to fly it, which most prefer. Hospitality at the Anantara starts from EUR 8,000 per couple or crew. Concours Croatia, held at the Boutique Hotel Alhambra on Losinj since 2024, runs 3 to 6 September at roughly half that.
articles.why: A principal entering a concours generates a logistics file, not a booking: shipping quotes, customs paperwork, insurance in transit, arrival windows and a car that must be presented immaculately at a set hour. This is concierge work of a high order.

briefs.b: Managing a smart house has moved from a rare skill to a standard requirement. In San Francisco, 83 per cent of household positions recruited in the past year required technical integration, with other cities following. New staff typically need 8 to 12 weeks to become comfortable with an unfamiliar household system.
briefs.src: Spear's, on the Morgan & Mallet Beyond the Butler 2025/26 report

briefs.b: At The Quail, the Peninsula-owned property near Carmel, last year's Best in Show was a track-restricted 1996 Ferrari F50 GT1 belonging to the Silicon Valley executive Art Zafiropoulo, who is reported to have turned down a USD 100 million offer for the car that day. The property has 93 guestrooms and was best known for its golf course until 2003.

Business jet manufacturers delivered 162 aircraft worldwide in the first quarter of 2026, almost 15 per cent more than a year earlier, with billings up 19 per cent to USD 6.1 billion. Embraer led the largest producers with deliveries up 26 per cent, and Pilatus nearly doubled PC-24 deliveries to nine. GAMA's second-quarter figures are due during the week of 24 August.
briefs.src: General Aviation Manufacturers Association (GAMA), quarterly shipments and billings

briefs.b: Average tenure across high-end household roles now sits at around three years, with nannies typically staying two to three, as staff become as mobile as the families they serve. Where the match is right, retention is markedly better: 92 per cent of personal assistants placed in Los Angeles by one agency stay beyond two years, as do the same proportion of nannies placed in Dubai.
briefs.src: Spear's, on the Morgan & Mallet Beyond the Butler 2025/26 report

lead.title: Family office pay is finally written down, and every role that serves the family acquires a number
lead.standfirst: New benchmarks put median total compensation at USD 900,000 for a chief investment officer and USD 825,000 for a chief executive, and for the first time the private household can see the ladder it stands beside.
lead.body:
For most of its history the family office has paid what it felt like paying. Packages were negotiated privately with the principal, rarely documented and almost never compared. That opacity is ending. The 2026 benchmarks now circulating among advisers, drawn from the Morgan Stanley and Botoff Consulting survey of United States investment focused single family offices, place median total compensation at USD 900,000 for a chief investment officer, USD 825,000 for a chief executive, USD 789,807 for a chief operating officer and USD 620,000 for a chief financial officer. At the other end of the same table, an analyst sits at USD 125,000 and a senior associate at USD 287,500. The whole structure of a household's professional apparatus is, for the first time, legible.

The numbers move sharply with size. Fidelity Family Office Services data shows a chief executive's base salary rising from USD 248,000 at an office below USD 250 million in assets to USD 550,000 above USD 1 billion, while a chief operating officer climbs from USD 175,000 to USD 276,000 across the same span. Region matters as much as scale. The most common chief executive band is USD 396,001 to USD 500,000 in the United States, GBP 198,001 to GBP 264,000 in the United Kingdom, and USD 330,001 to USD 396,000 in the United Arab Emirates, according to the KPMG Private Enterprise and Agreus Group benchmark. A family that moves its office from London to Dubai is not simply changing jurisdiction · it is changing the price of its own staff.

The structure of pay is shifting too. Roughly 90 per cent of offices now offer an annual incentive, and about 62 per cent of investment focused single family offices run a long term vehicle. In 2025, co-investment opportunities at 57 per cent overtook deferred incentive compensation at 56 per cent for the first time since 2015. Above roughly USD 1 billion in assets, some 70 per cent of offices operate a formal long term incentive plan, rising to about 73 per cent above USD 2.5 billion. The market has quietly decided that a competitive base salary alone will no longer hold a senior professional against private equity.

Behind the tables sits a shortage. At a Katten programme in May, Brian Adams of Mack International described a substantial uptick in activity driven by newly created offices and by baby boomer succession, with chief financial officer roles the hardest to fill. More than a third of offices in Botoff's 2026 planning survey reported recruiting difficulty in the past year, and larger offices reported more. Trish Botoff's conclusion was blunt: an office that has not revisited its pay structure recently is probably already behind the market.

None of these tables include the house. The estate manager, the principal's private assistant, the head of security and the travelling chef are almost never benchmarked in the same document as the chief financial officer, even when they report into the same person and hold considerably more of the family's daily trust. But the two ladders are converging. As offices formalise pay, the household is increasingly asked to justify its own on the same terms, with written scope, documented incentives and a stated compensation philosophy rather than the older arrangement of a good salary and a quiet understanding.
lead.why: The household is being drawn into the same compensation conversation as the family office. Knowing what the office beside you earns, and how its pay is structured, is now part of negotiating your own position with credibility.
lead.src: Simple, Family Office Compensation and Salary Guide 2026

articles.title: Protection moves from the boardroom into the household, and the person who books the car now works alongside a detail
articles.body:
The share of American executives receiving formal protection has risen from 24.5 per cent in 2023 to about 37 per cent by mid-2026, and median annual spending per protected executive climbed from USD 69,000 in 2023 to USD 94,000 in 2024. What began as a corporate line item has crossed into the private household, where the same principal who travels with a detail on business now expects continuity at home, on holiday and on the school run.

The cost structure is unforgiving. Individual officers bill from USD 75 to USD 200 an hour. A full operation for a high profile principal runs from USD 500,000 to USD 3 million a year, and families with a documented kidnap risk can reach from USD 1.5 million to more than USD 5 million. Compensation for the people inside those operations has risen accordingly: a detail agent sits at roughly USD 128,000 base at the median in the United States national market, a detail leader at USD 185,000 and a director of security at USD 230,000.

Demand accelerated after the killing of a major American chief executive in late 2024. Recruiters reported demand for certified protection personnel up around 75 per cent year on year and ad hoc travel security up roughly 300 per cent. The consequence for staffing is familiar to anyone who has tried to hire a house manager this year: the qualified candidates are already placed, and the families competing for them are willing to pay above the published band.

For the house, the arrival of a permanent security function changes the shape of the job. Guest lists, deliveries, contractor access, travel manifests and the movement of children through the day all become shared information. The estate manager who once controlled the diary alone now co-ordinates it with a head of security who holds a veto. The households that work best are those where that boundary is written down in advance rather than discovered during an incident.
articles.why: Security is becoming a standing department in the private household rather than an occasional supplier. Knowing how a detail is staffed, priced and integrated with the diary is now part of running an estate competently.
articles.src: Talent Gurus, UHNW Executive Protection Salaries 2026

articles.title: Global private jet departures pass 78,000 in a single week, and Europe's August rhythm becomes visible in the data
articles.body:
In the week ending 9 August 2026, private aircraft worldwide recorded more than 78,000 departures, a rise of 2.3 per cent on the same week of 2025, carried largely by a 4 per cent gain in United States flights. Europe accounted for close to 13,000 of those departures, roughly 1 per cent above last year but 12 per cent below the previous week.

The week on week fall is the more instructive figure. The United Kingdom dropped 12 per cent, France 21 per cent and Italy 19 per cent. This is not a market weakening · it is the great August stillness, the point at which families stop moving because they have already arrived. The aircraft that flew heavily through late July into Nice, Olbia and Ibiza are now parked, waiting for the return leg.

The wider European season has been softer than the headline suggests. In the week to mid-July, Europe recorded 10,792 fractional and charter flights, about 4 per cent below the same week a year earlier, with Germany and Italy each down around 10 per cent. Germany was 8 per cent below last year again in the second week of August. By contrast, mid-May saw more than 11,000 European departures, 3 per cent up year on year. The pattern of 2026 is a strong spring, a flat high summer and an American market doing most of the growing.

For whoever manages the family's movement, the operational point is the reverse of the traffic curve. Quiet skies in mid-August mean crew rest, maintenance slots and repositioning capacity are available at short notice, while the last ten days of the month, when everyone returns at once, are the hardest of the year to charter into northern Europe. The competent household books the September return before it books the August arrival.
articles.why: Flight data is the closest thing the private world has to a public calendar. Reading it tells a household when aircraft, crew and slots are scarce, and when they can be secured cheaply.
articles.src: Private Jet Card Comparisons, WingX flight activity analysis, week 32

articles.title: The branded residence passes 900 schemes worldwide, and the private house arrives with a service manual attached
articles.body:
There were 323 branded residential schemes in the world in 2015. By the end of 2025 there were around 910, a rise of 19 per cent on the 764 counted in December 2024 and a compound annual growth rate of 10.9 per cent, faster than either global hospitality or global real estate over the same decade. The confirmed pipeline runs to 1,747 developments by 2032.

The growth is also broadening. During 2025 alone, 25 countries recorded their first branded residential project, joined by 39 new hotel brands and 19 new non-hotel brands entering the sector. Asia Pacific has expanded by 55 per cent over five years, driven by Vietnam, Thailand and India. The buyer pays for the arrangement: branded homes carry an average price premium of 33 per cent over comparable unbranded stock worldwide, rising to 39 per cent in resort locations.

What the premium buys is not architecture. It is service, standardised and contractually guaranteed · housekeeping to a published specification, a concierge desk, security, maintenance, and in the better schemes a residence manager who holds the same operational responsibilities as a private estate manager. For a family with five houses, a branded residence is the one address that runs itself.

That has a double consequence for anyone in private service. It creates a large and growing employer of exactly the skills the private household needs, with clearer career structure and published standards than most single family posts offer. It also raises the bar inside the private house, because a principal who has lived under a branded service specification in Dubai or Bangkok arrives at their own estate expecting the same consistency from a staff of four.
articles.why: Branded residences are becoming both a competitor for private service talent and the benchmark against which principals silently measure their own households. Understanding how they are staffed and specified is now professional literacy.

articles.title: Fine wine stops falling, American buyers take a quarter of the market, and the cellar becomes worth reading again
articles.body:
After three years in which fine wine was the quietest embarrassment in the collecting world, Liv-ex's report on the first half of 2026 finds prices stabilising rather than sliding. Indices held broadly flat through the first quarter, though they posted their first declines since the previous August during March, and the Fine Wine 50, which tracks the Bordeaux first growths, rose 0.7 per cent over the four months to 30 April.

The geography of demand has shifted. United States buyers accounted for more than a quarter of purchase value on the exchange in the second quarter, and their share has risen steadily through the year. Trade value and volume both sit above the 2025 average, if still below where they stood in the first quarter of 2025. Older Bordeaux, long the most punished part of the market, has found firmer footing, and Italian wines have led the broader recovery, with Champagne also drawing renewed interest.

Nobody in the trade is calling it a rally. The consensus is that the market will bump along the bottom through 2026, and Liv-ex itself has described the recovery as only at its start. What that means in practice is that Bordeaux is available at its lowest prices since 2020, a fact that collectors and, more tellingly, drinkers have begun to act on.

For the household, a soft market is an opportunity and a duty. Cellars bought at the 2021 peak are worth less on paper than their insurance schedules suggest, and valuations more than two years old are now materially wrong. The households that handle this well are those where someone keeps a current inventory, checks provenance and storage records, and knows which cases are for the table and which are collateral.
articles.why: Cellar management is one of the few genuinely technical responsibilities that lands on a house manager. A stabilising market makes accurate inventory, valuation and insurance schedules newly urgent.

briefs.b: The world's largest concentration of superyachts is in the Mediterranean, moving between St Tropez, Mallorca, Mykonos, Sardinia and the Amalfi Coast. Among the summer's notable sightings was Pure, an 82 metre yacht built by the Devonport yard in the United Kingdom, seen off St Tropez on 24 July.

Household staffing benchmarks for 2026 put the median United States estate manager at about USD 185,000. Entry level posts begin around USD 85,000 to USD 120,000, while senior managers with ten years or more reach USD 180,000 to USD 250,000 before benefits.
briefs.src: Talent Gurus, Household Staff Salary and Compensation Guide 2026

briefs.b: Liv-ex has published its closing report on the 2025 en primeur campaign, concluding that the vintage may prove better than the market currently believes. The campaign was released into a Bordeaux market still trading near its lowest levels since 2020.

Knight Frank expects average prime residential price growth across 20 global cities to rise from 1.6 per cent in 2026 to 2.2 per cent in 2027. Global luxury residential prices grew 3.2 per cent in 2025, slightly below the 3.6 per cent recorded in 2024, with Middle Eastern markets leading and North America the only region in negative territory.

lead.title: A chauffeur company takes New York to court over the trip log, and the movements of the wealthy become a constitutional question
lead.standfirst: Wheely argues that a city rule requiring every journey to be recorded to within three feet, and then kept indefinitely, quietly builds a permanent surveillance file on the people it drives.
lead.body:
The rule at the centre of the case is administrative rather than dramatic. Every licensed for-hire vehicle operator in New York City must submit a monthly, unaggregated record of each trip taken. That record includes pickup and drop-off locations to within three feet, the exact timing of the journey, and driver and vehicle details. The data is retained indefinitely. Wheely, a chauffeur service founded in London in 2012 and now operating in Paris, Dubai and New York, went to court almost as soon as it entered the New York market in the spring, arguing that the requirement amounts to a warrantless and permanent record of its clients' movements. A judge in the Southern District of New York dismissed the claim in April 2026. The case is now before the Second Circuit Court of Appeals.

Anton Chirkunov, the company's chief executive, told Spear's that the exposure is not evenly distributed. "Privacy is an asymmetrical risk for the wealthy," he said, citing doxxing and the consequences of government data being shared, leaked or stolen. "A record of a person's rides is a record of their life," he added, pointing to the business meetings they take, the homes they return to and the schools their children attend. The New York City Taxi and Limousine Commission says the trip log rule is necessary to enforce driver fatigue and passenger safety requirements, and that it takes its responsibility to protect the data seriously.

The precedent that hangs over the argument is a decade old. In 2014 the city released 173 million taxi trip records under a public records request. The records were not sufficiently anonymised, and researchers were able to reverse the process using publicly available photographs and celebrity gossip blogs. One analyst traced a specific 2013 ride taken by the actor Bradley Cooper, down to a fare of USD 10.50 with no recorded tip. The episode is remembered as a curiosity. The lesson underneath it is that a large enough movement dataset does not stay anonymous for long.

Security practitioners describe a more serious version of the same problem. Mike O'Neill, managing director of the security firm Optimal Risk, told Spear's that repeated pickup and drop-off locations can be analysed to identify a client's home address, office, family residences, schools and gyms with a high degree of confidence. Once that pattern is established, he said, a threat actor can begin to predict where an individual is likely to be at a specific date and time. He warned that agentic artificial intelligence tools could automate this kind of pattern analysis at scale, creating openings for surveillance, stalking and kidnapping, and making burglary less risky during known absences. Cameron Colquhoun, chief executive of the cybersecurity firm Neon Century, added that with the right open source intelligence, anonymised data can be reverse engineered relatively easily.

Wheely's own model reads as a catalogue of private service discipline. Drivers train at what the company calls a chauffeur academy, sign non-disclosure agreements, and operate without CCTV inside the vehicle. Chirkunov says clients speak on the telephone in the car in a way they do not in conventional black cars. The company withdrew its product from app stores in Russia in 2020 rather than comply with local data rules, and Chirkunov says he is prepared to take the New York challenge to the Supreme Court. "The question is not whether it leaks," he said, "but when."
lead.why: A family's movements are now a dataset, and someone in the household creates it every day by booking cars, flights and school runs. Knowing which suppliers record, retain and sell journey data is becoming as much a part of the role as knowing which florist to call.

articles.title: Three in four family businesses have been attacked, and the people who answer the telephone are now part of the defence
articles.body:
Deloitte Private's Family business cybersecurity 2026, published on 29 January as part of its family business insights series, puts a number on something the private world has preferred to discuss quietly. Nearly three quarters of family businesses globally, 74 per cent, have faced at least one cyberattack in the past two years. A third, 33 per cent, have experienced two or more. Exposure is close to universal by region. Asia Pacific leads on frequency with 90 per cent reporting at least one attack, North America follows at 77 per cent, and even the lowest region, South America, records 61 per cent.

The shape of those attacks matters more to a household than the headline. Malware was reported by 49 per cent of respondents and phishing or business email compromise by 48 per cent, but the next three categories are the ones that arrive through people rather than through servers. Social engineering was experienced by 43 per cent, third-party risk by 40 per cent and insider threats by 27 per cent. Each of those routes runs through someone who has been trusted with access: a supplier, a contractor, an assistant, a member of staff.

Defences have not kept pace. Only 43 per cent of family businesses report a robust cybersecurity strategy that has never failed them. Of the rest, 49 per cent describe a strategy with noticeable gaps and 8 per cent have none at all, and 48 per cent feel only moderately prepared or not at all prepared should an attack land. Basic controls are widespread: software updates at 59 per cent, network security and multi-factor authentication at 57 per cent each, data backups at 48 per cent. The more advanced measures lag badly. Incident response playbooks appear in 40 per cent of cases, cyber maturity assessments in 36 per cent, vendor governance in 32 per cent and identity management in 31 per cent.

The consequences are now routine rather than exceptional. Among those targeted, 54 per cent suffered financial harm, 51 per cent operational harm and 51 per cent reputational harm. Only 4 per cent of respondents globally reported no loss or damage of any kind. For a family that owns the business, the reputational column is not an abstraction, because the family name is the brand and the household is where the family name lives.

The practical translation for private service is narrow and useful. Vendor governance and identity management are the two weakest controls in the survey, and both are exercised daily inside a house: who is on the approved supplier list, who is admitted, who is given a code, who is allowed to change a bank detail on an invoice. A household that verifies payment instructions by voice on a known number, keeps a written contractor register and rehearses what happens when a convincing message arrives at nine on a Friday evening is running a control the family business itself may not have.
articles.why: Social engineering and third-party risk reach the household long before they reach the family office. The person who checks a payment instruction, verifies a delivery or refuses an unscheduled contractor is operating a security control, not performing a courtesy.

articles.title: Hackers copy Liechtenstein's register of beneficial owners, and the names behind 31,000 structures walk out of the door
articles.body:
During the night of 29 to 30 July, unknown perpetrators gained unauthorised access to Liechtenstein's register of beneficial owners and copied data relating to around 31,000 companies, foundations and trusts. Irregularities were detected and the affected system was taken offline. The government convened a crisis unit on the Saturday evening, headed by the prime minister, Brigitte Haas, and the minister of justice, Emanuel Schadler. On the current state of knowledge, there is no indication that data in the system was modified or deleted. It was copied.

The register itself was created in 2021, under Liechtenstein's Act on the Register of the Beneficial Owners of Legal Entities, and is maintained by the Office of Justice for the purpose of preventing money laundering and terrorist financing. Its whole design is to strip away layers of corporate opacity and record, in one place, the natural persons who ultimately stand behind a legal structure. That is exactly what makes the file valuable to anyone who should not have it.

Liechtenstein matters here out of all proportion to its size. The Principality is one of Europe's principal jurisdictions for private foundations and trust structures, instruments used by families to hold operating businesses, art, property and succession arrangements across generations. A register of beneficial owners in Vaduz is, in effect, an index of a certain kind of European and international private wealth, with names attached.

The breach lands in a season in which the private world has been arguing about who holds its data and how long they hold it. The trip log dispute in New York turns on the same principle, that information collected for a legitimate administrative purpose becomes a hazard the moment it is aggregated, retained and connected to an identity. Registers of this kind are mandated by law and cannot be opted out of, which removes the usual defence of choosing discreet suppliers.

For those who work close to a family, the immediate lesson is not technical. It is that the paper trail is now the exposed surface. A structure that is invisible in public can still be legible in a government file, and that file can be copied in a single night.
articles.why: Discretion has moved beyond what staff say to who holds the family's name in writing. Anyone who completes forms, engages suppliers or files documents on a family's behalf is deciding, in small increments, how many registers carry that name.

articles.title: Monaco's average price passes 57,000 euros a square metre, and the long-term renters finally decide to buy
articles.body:
Savills' Spotlight on Monaco 2026 records an average price of EUR 57,569 per square metre across the Principality, roughly GBP 4,600 per square foot. Larvotto has passed EUR 70,000 per square metre for the first time, around GBP 5,600 per square foot, a figure driven largely by units at Mareterra, the ultra-prime development launched in December 2024, entering the market. Kelcie Sellers, who leads global residential research at Savills, described the effect plainly: "This has rewritten the rule book on what is considered ultra-prime in Monaco."

The defining constraint has not changed. Monaco occupies just over two square kilometres, and Sellers says the pipeline for new construction is now "basically zero". Total transaction value held steady at EUR 5.9 billion, but that stability conceals a shift in where the activity sits. New build has receded and resale has taken over, rising sharply in both volume and value in 2025. Sellers characterises this as a return to normal after the Mareterra cycle, which she calls a temporary disruption in an otherwise resale-led market.

Within the resale segment, demand has concentrated on size. Four-bedroom homes have seen some of the strongest price appreciation, with average values rising more than 50 per cent, while ultra-prime resales above EUR 20 million reached record levels. Irene Luke, co-head of Savills Monaco, put the buyer logic simply: "The bigger the apartment, the better it is for buyers." She attributes the shift to Monaco's evolution from a fiscal base into a place people actually live. "Monaco has become a lot more sophisticated. The schooling is better, healthcare is better."

The supporting detail is domestic rather than financial. A new British school opened in 2022, alongside the established presence of the International School of Monaco. Nice airport, around 30 minutes away by road, keeps adding transatlantic routes and European links. Sellers notes that remote working convinced buyers they could run global businesses from the Principality, and they have been upgrading into larger homes accordingly.

The rental market is pushing in the same direction. Supply shortages have driven rents up more than 9 per cent over the past year, and properties are frequently secured before they reach the open market. Luke reports the consequence in client behaviour: "Long-term renters finally are thinking that they should really buy something."
articles.why: A four-bedroom principal residence occupied full time is a different brief from a pied-a-terre visited for the Grand Prix. It requires a rota, a supplier book, school-run logistics and a handover file, which is why Monaco households increasingly recruit for permanence rather than for the season.
articles.src: Savills, Spotlight on Monaco 2026, reported by Spear's

articles.title: 43 yachts delivered this year gather in Port Hercule, and the yards behind them are sold out to 2029
articles.body:
The Monaco Yacht Show has published the first official list of superyachts confirmed for its 35th edition, which runs in Port Hercule from 23 to 26 September. Around 120 vessels are expected by opening day, and 43 of the yachts on the initial list are due for delivery during 2026. Toby Moore, chief executive of Informa Prestige, which organises the show, framed the appeal in logistical terms: "In four days and in a single harbour, you can walk the decks of 43 yachts delivering this year."

The largest new delivery on the current list is the 102 metre Nixie, built by Lurssen, and the smallest is Arcadia's A80 at 23.98 metres. Between them sit Damen Yachting's 80 metre Pangea and 60 metre QU2, Sanlorenzo's 73.4 metre Silver Fox and Isa Yachts' 66.4 metre Sea Raider X. The segment from 40 to 60 metres is well represented, with Benetti's B.Now 50M, Riva's 54 Metri, Baglietto's Fast50 and T60, Tankoa's Singolare, Gulf Craft's Majesty 145 and Sirena Marine's Sirena Superyacht 42 Metre. Italian builders account for much of the confirmed fleet, including Sanlorenzo, Azimut-Benetti and brands within the Ferretti Group. Sailing yachts, multihulls, recently refitted vessels and brokerage yachts complete the list, with more names due before September.

The context behind the fleet is a market that is contracting in count and expanding in scale. BOAT International's Global Order Book 2026 reports that the number of yachts on order has declined for a second consecutive year, while average yacht size continues to increase and build slots at the leading shipyards are largely committed until 2028 to 2029. The industry is not building more boats. It is building bigger ones, and it has already sold the next three years of capacity.

That combination has a direct effect below deck. Every one of the 43 new hulls arriving this year requires a crew, an interior standard, a provisioning chain and a shoreside team, and larger average tonnage means larger complements per vessel. A fleet growing by size rather than by number still increases total demand for people, and it does so in the specific direction of senior, experienced crew capable of running a 60 metre programme rather than a 30 metre one.
articles.why: Yachts and houses draw on the same shrinking pool of trained private staff, and a rising average length means each new delivery absorbs more of it. For anyone building a career on the interior side, the growth is at the top of the size range, where standards and expectations are highest.

articles.title: Swiss watch exports hold at CHF 12.2 billion for the half year, and all the growth arrives at the bottom of the price list
articles.body:
The Federation of the Swiss Watch Industry published its half year statistics on 21 July. Exports of wristwatches declined slightly, by 0.6 per cent, to CHF 12.2 billion over the first six months of 2026. Volumes moved the other way. More than 7 million watches were shipped abroad in the period, an increase of 162,000 units on the first half of 2025, or 2.3 per cent. More watches left Switzerland, and they were worth marginally less.

The explanation sits in the price bands. Volume growth was driven mainly by mechanical watches with an export price below CHF 500, a category up 23.8 per cent. The drag on value came from the segment running from CHF 500 to CHF 3,000, down 5.7 per cent. The industry is selling more of its cheapest mechanical product and less of the middle, which is where a great deal of the industry's revenue traditionally lives.

The monthly pattern within the half is worth holding separately from the total. June was strong, with exports up 11.2 per cent to nearly CHF 2.4 billion and volumes up 11.7 per cent to 1.3 million pieces. That single month partly rescued a soft first quarter. The comparison base is a full year 2025 in which Swiss watch exports fell 1.7 per cent to CHF 25.5 billion, so a flat half year represents stabilisation rather than recovery.

This is a different signal from the one the salerooms have been sending. Auction results have been carried by trophy lots and by demand for independent makers, a narrow market of scarce pieces. The export figures describe the wide market of new product moving through retail, and the two can diverge for long periods. A collection can be appreciating while the industry that produced it is flat.

For anyone whose work touches a principal's collection, the useful discipline is to read both. Insurance valuations, service intervals and the question of whether a piece should be worn, stored or sold all sit at the intersection of a retail market that is soft in the middle and a secondary market that is selective at the top.
articles.why: Cultural fluency means being able to distinguish an auction headline from a trade statistic. A principal who mentions the watch market may be talking about either, and knowing which one is moving is part of holding the conversation properly.
articles.src: Federation of the Swiss Watch Industry, half year statistics, 21 July 2026

briefs.b: A proposed maximum police response time of 20 minutes for rural emergencies could leave country estates exposed, security advisers have told Spear's, with organised crime groups increasingly targeting isolated houses, farms and outbuildings. The National Farmers' Union puts the cost of rural crime at GBP 44.1 million in 2025, down 16.5 per cent from GBP 52.8 million in 2023, a decline that greater police focus has driven but that the growing sophistication of those groups now threatens.

Aldar has activated the final phase of the Saadiyat Island masterplan with Marsa Al Saadiyat, a waterfront district carrying a gross development value of AED 100 billion, around USD 27.2 billion. It covers 6.4 million square metres, is planned for more than 58,000 residents across private mansions, villas, waterfront apartments and branded residences, and includes a marina with more than 350 berths. The first homes go on sale in the second half of 2026.

Yachts above 50 metres were largely committed for July and August by early spring, and berths in Monaco, Saint-Tropez, Porto Cervo and Mykonos are secured well in advance of the season. Brokers report demand outpacing supply in Mallorca, Ibiza, the Amalfi Coast and the Cyclades, with June and September offering similar conditions and considerably more flexibility on where a boat can stop.

Bvlgari Resort Ranfushi is due to open in Raa Atoll in the Maldives, around 45 minutes by seaplane from Male, across roughly 20 hectares. The property is planned with 54 villas and suites in total, including 33 beach villas with private pools, 20 overwater villas and a Bulgari Villa set on its own island. It is the group's tenth hotel and only its second resort.

lead.title: The inheriting generation says the responsibility arrives before the money, and USD 83 trillion is waiting behind it
lead.standfirst: UBS has surveyed more than 170 members of the world's inheriting families and found a generation already inside the family enterprise, well informed about the wealth, and impatient with the silence that surrounds it.
lead.body:
The Global Next Generation Report 2026, published by UBS, rests on two surveys of members of the Young Investors Organization, one conducted in May 2025 and a second between December 2025 and January 2026, together with ten deep interviews carried out between 22 October and 29 December 2025. More than 170 responses were gathered in total. Europe supplied 49 per cent of respondents, North America 19 per cent, Latin America 16 per cent, Asia-Pacific 11 per cent and the Middle East and Africa 5 per cent. Most are aged between 26 and 40. Just over half already work inside the family business or the family office, about one in ten have founded ventures of their own, and the remaining third are employed elsewhere, studying, or still deciding.

The headline finding is a question of language. Asked what they associate most with wealth transfer, 41 per cent chose a shift of responsibility and 38 per cent chose the death of a family member. The split follows geography closely. In North America 67 per cent framed the moment as responsibility. In Asia-Pacific and Latin America around 60 per cent framed it as a bereavement. It also follows generational depth: among second and third generation families roughly 40 per cent think first of a death, a figure that falls to just above 20 per cent by the fourth generation, while the share thinking first of responsibility rises to 50 per cent among fourth and fifth generations. Behind all of it sits an estimated USD 83 trillion of private wealth expected to change hands worldwide over the next two to three decades.

The machinery is thinner than the rhetoric. Six in ten families have a will and around half have a legal and tax succession structure, but fewer than a quarter have formal governance, meaning defined family roles, written constitutions and agreed communication protocols. Nearly half, 48 per cent, say the generation before them had no structured transfer process at all, and 17 per cent simply do not know. When disagreements arise, 56 per cent address them informally as they occur and 35 per cent defer to a senior family figure. Communication failure is the single largest source of conflict at 33 per cent, ahead of disagreements about lifestyle, spending or work ethics at 27 per cent, differing views of fairness at 24 per cent and unclear roles at 16 per cent. Families that do have governance move faster: 74 per cent of those with strong processes are already planning or transferring.

Institutions are arriving to fill the gap. Thirty-seven per cent of respondents now manage their wealth through a single family office, 29 per cent through a wealth manager or private bank and 27 per cent directly. The generational gradient is stark: around 30 per cent of second generation families use a single family office, rising to 75 per cent by the fourth. Parents still open 60 per cent of transfer conversations, but as the process unfolds the next generation's share of driving it rises from 13 per cent to 22 per cent while the current generation's falls to 43 per cent. Fifty-six per cent believe the conversation should begin before the age of twenty, against the 17 per cent who actually first discussed wealth in childhood.

Their expectations of the people who serve them are equally explicit. Seventy-nine per cent want demonstrable expertise from an adviser, 56 per cent want a relationship that works across generations and 67 per cent say a strong personal connection matters. Eighty-three per cent want a blend of digital and in-person contact rather than one or the other. Among the services that make a provider stand out, networking is cited by 78 per cent, legal and tax support by 56 per cent and education by 29 per cent.
lead.why: The people who will sign the household contracts of the next thirty years are already in the room, and half of them are already working inside the family structure. They arrive with more advisers, more documentation and less tolerance for improvisation, which means the households they inherit will increasingly be judged on records, protocols and continuity rather than on personal loyalty alone.

articles.title: Britain rewrites the rules for anyone who employs staff at home, and the private household becomes an employer like any other
articles.body:
The Employment Rights Act 2025 has been arriving in stages, and the April 2026 tranche is the one that touches every private household with a payroll. Statutory sick pay reform took effect: the lower earnings limit of GBP 129 in average weekly earnings has been removed, so lower-paid employees are now entitled to sick pay worth 80 per cent of their wages, and the waiting period has gone, meaning sick pay is due from the first day of absence rather than the fourth. Paternity leave and unpaid parental leave became day one rights, as did bereaved partner's paternity leave, which entitles a father or partner to take up to 52 weeks where the mother or primary caregiver dies.

A quieter change may prove the most consequential for estate offices. On 6 April 2026, implementing regulations introduced without prior indication a duty on employers to keep records of both annual leave entitlement and holiday pay, and to retain those records for six years. Employers who fail to keep records adequate to show compliance commit an offence punishable by a fine. For a household that has historically managed rotas on a shared calendar and settled holiday informally at the kitchen table, this is a documentary obligation with teeth.

More is scheduled. From 1 October 2026 the time limit for bringing most employment tribunal claims doubles from three months to six. From 30 October 2026 the workplace harassment reforms bite, including the duty to take all reasonable steps to prevent harassment and liability for harassment by third parties, a provision with obvious implications for houses that receive contractors, suppliers and guests. From 1 January 2027 the qualifying period for ordinary unfair dismissal falls from two years to six months, which in practice captures anyone engaged from 1 July 2026 onward, and the cap on unfair dismissal compensation is removed for terminations on or after that date. Pinsent Masons notes that the removal of the cap is significant for high earners and their employers.

The cumulative effect is that the informality which has long characterised domestic employment is being legislated out of existence. Contracts, payslips, written rotas, holiday records, grievance routes and a documented approach to harassment are no longer marks of an unusually organised house. They are the statutory minimum, and the person who holds them together is almost always the house or estate manager.
articles.why: Household employers are employers in law, and the paperwork that proves it now sits with whoever runs the house. A candidate who can arrive with a working knowledge of records, notice periods and the new dismissal timetable is offering the family risk management, not just service.

articles.title: The non-dom register shrinks by 1,200 in its final year, and London's biggest houses change hands anyway
articles.body:
HMRC released figures at the end of July covering the last full year of the non-domiciled regime, a status that had existed in British tax law since 1799, when it was created to shelter colonial investments. The number of non-dom taxpayers, including those deemed domiciled, fell by 1,200 from 83,100 to 81,900, a decline of 1 per cent. About 9,000 left during the 2024 to 2025 tax year against 11,200 the year before, while arrivals dropped from 10,000 to roughly 8,600. In the same period the group paid GBP 9.7 billion, about USD 13 billion, in capital gains, employment and income taxes, an increase of 9 per cent and the largest total in records going back to 2008.

The figures predate the reform itself. The regime was replaced in April 2025 with a residence-based system under which arrivals are exempt from tax on foreign income and gains for four years before being taxed as ordinary residents, and under which wealth held abroad is brought into the inheritance tax net. The government has said it will only be able to estimate departures since that change next year. It projects around GBP 33 billion in additional revenue over the coming years, a figure several research bodies dispute. Among those who have left are the Checkout.com founder Guillaume Pousaz and the Egyptian industrialist Nassef Sawiris. Italy and Greece have both built regimes designed to receive them.

The property data reads two ways at once. Across the twelve months following the April 2025 change, transactions in prime central London fell by more than 32 per cent and prices by 7 per cent, according to LonRes. Activity is down at every price point compared with each of the previous five years, with one exception: the band above GBP 30 million. Beauchamp Estates counts 34 sales above GBP 15 million in the first half of 2026, worth a combined GBP 1.24 billion, an increase of more than 78 per cent on the same period last year.

The individual deals explain the skew. Providence House in Chelsea sold for GBP 270 million, a record, in a sealed-bid process. The Holme in Regent's Park, a 40-room stucco mansion, sold for GBP 195 million, roughly 40 per cent above the price it fetched less than eighteen months earlier. Beauchamp's Rosy Khalastchy notes that a buyer at GBP 15 million and above typically has a net worth of at least GBP 100 million and a portfolio of houses across several cities, and may spend only a few weeks a year in London. Savills' Richard Gutteridge puts it plainly: extreme wealth may change where it resides most or least, but not where it chooses to buy.
articles.why: A house owned by someone who lives elsewhere is still a house that has to run. Fewer resident principals and more intermittently occupied trophy properties shifts the private service brief toward standing readiness, security, contractor supervision and the ability to bring a closed house to full operation at short notice.

articles.title: The pre-owned aircraft shelf empties, and the family that wants a large-cabin jet now joins a queue
articles.body:
AMSTAT's second quarter analysis, published at the start of August, records a market that is busy and bare at the same time. Pre-owned transactions rose 11.2 per cent year on year in the quarter and ran 14 per cent above the ten-year average for the period. Yet listed turbine inventory stood at just 5.8 per cent of the active fleet at the end of June, the lowest reading since February 2024 and well below the ten-year average of 7.2 per cent. For jets specifically, 6.5 per cent of the fleet is for sale against a norm of 8.1 per cent.

The squeeze is sharpest at the top. Heavy jet transactions rose 43.8 per cent year on year, by a wide margin the strongest performance of any category, though the comparison flatters somewhat because the same quarter last year was unusually soft for large cabins. With only 5.2 per cent of the heavy fleet listed, the pricing signal to owners of late-model aircraft is unambiguous. Super-midsize activity, led by the Challenger 300 and the Gulfstream G280, was roughly flat, which leaves buyers in that segment more room to negotiate.

Headline asking prices tell a misleading story. They have fallen across several segments, which at a glance suggests cooling. Median transaction values, meaning what aircraft actually sold for, are up 5 per cent year on year and 2 per cent since January. The divergence reflects a two-speed market: younger, higher-value jets sell quickly, while older airframes sit and are discounted.

None of this resolves quickly. Manufacturers continue to face production constraints, and new aircraft supply is expected to remain tight through 2027 at best, which keeps pressure on the late-model pre-owned market. For anyone advising a family on how it flies, the practical consequence is a longer lead time and a stronger case for charter, fractional shares or a managed arrangement in the interim.
articles.why: The person who builds the family's travel calendar needs to know that an aircraft is no longer something that can be acquired on a whim. Understanding lead times, charter fallbacks and the difference between an owned, managed and fractional arrangement is now part of the logistical vocabulary of private service.
articles.src: GlobalAir.com, on AMSTAT Q2 2026 data, 4 August 2026

articles.title: Monterey heads for the first half-billion-dollar auction week in collecting history, and the buyers are getting younger
articles.body:
The auctions that punctuate Monterey Car Week are forecast to take between USD 470 million and USD 500 million this year, according to Hagerty, which would surpass the all-time record of USD 471 million set in 2022. "With strong bidding, this could be the first half-billion-dollar auction week the collector world has ever seen," said the company's chief executive, McKeel Hagerty. The sales run through to 15 August.

The most expensive lot of the week is a 1996 McLaren F1 GTR, offered by RM Sotheby's on 15 August with an estimate in excess of USD 35 million. It is the only example finished in the factory's scarlet and yellow pop art livery, and it spent twenty-five years in the collection of the Pink Floyd drummer Nick Mason before changing hands quietly in 2024.

What is moving the market is a change of taste rather than a change of temperature. The Hagerty Supercar Index has risen 30 per cent over the past twelve months while the Blue Chip Index, which tracks the traditional pillars of the collector market, has fallen 2 per cent. Demand is being driven by Millennial and Gen Z buyers who are not competing for the 1950s and 1960s machinery their parents pursued, but bidding up the modern supercars of their own adolescence.

That divergence matters beyond the auction tent. A collection assembled on the assumptions of twenty years ago now contains two quite different asset classes, one appreciating on nostalgia and one drifting. The households that hold these cars are increasingly asked to think about storage conditions, event entries, transport logistics and insurance valuations that move faster than an annual review can capture.
articles.why: Cars are among the possessions a principal is most likely to discuss in company, and the person who arranges their movement, storage and entry to events needs the vocabulary to do so credibly. Knowing why a supercar index is outrunning a blue chip index is cultural fluency, not trivia.

articles.title: The salerooms recover their nerve with USD 6.8 billion in six months, and collections quietly become collateral
articles.body: Christie's, Sotheby's and Phillips together took USD 6.8 billion at auction in the first half of 2026, a rise of 70 per cent year on year and the strongest first half since 2022. Christie's reported half-year revenue of USD 4.5 billion, with public auction sales up 71 per cent at USD 3.5 billion and a sell-through rate of 91 per cent by lot. Sotheby's posted public auction sales of USD 3.4 billion, up 59 per cent, and total turnover of USD 4.4 billion including a record USD 826 million of private sales. Phillips rose 60 per cent to USD 507 million. Single-owner collections did much of the work. The S.I. Newhouse collection totalled USD 630.8 million at Christie's in New York in May and produced the two highest prices of the year so far, Jackson Pollock's Number 7A at USD 181.2 million and Constantin Brancusi's Danaide at USD 107.6 million. Sotheby's sold the Joe Lewis collection in London in June for USD 406.2 million, the highest total for any sale of Impressionist, Modern and contemporary art ever staged in Europe. The more revealing development sits behind the results. Both houses are expanding art-backed lending. Sotheby's completed a USD 900 million securitisation in January, bundling art loans into tradable notes, and for the first time the issue included loans secured against collectible cars. Christie's reports clients borrowing against cars, handbags, watches and, increasingly, wine. Its chief executive Bonnie Brennan notes that many finance clients are in no way short of capital and are simply optimising how they use it, often reinvesting in art. The audience is also changing shape. Forty-seven per cent of Christie's new clients this year are Millennial or Gen Z, and 85 per cent of its bids came in online. Luxury, meaning watches, jewellery, cars, handbags and memorabilia, is now the second largest category at both houses and functions as the entry point for those buyers. Once a collection is pledged against a loan, its condition, location and documentation stop being matters of taste and become matters of covenant. Provenance files, condition reports, storage conditions and movement records acquire a financial as well as a curatorial function.
articles.why: When a family borrows against its pictures, cars or wine, the household records that describe those objects become part of a credit file. The staff who log, insure, store and move them are handling balance-sheet assets, and accuracy is no longer a courtesy.

briefs.t: Europe slips as the jets fly on
briefs.b: Global business aviation flight activity rose 5.6 per cent year on year in July, according to Argus, with North America powering the increase and turboprops leading the surge there. Europe recorded its first yearly decline in fourteen months.

Multi-property estate managers now sit at a median of USD 280,000 and face a counter-offer rate of 52 per cent, the highest of any household role, with offer acceptance at just 56 per cent. Signing bonuses appear in 45 per cent of placements, from USD 20,000 to USD 45,000. Demand for personal assistants is growing fastest of all, at 22 per cent a year.
briefs.src: Talent Gurus, Household Staff Salary Guide 2026

briefs.b: Millennials and Gen Z now account for roughly a third of watch bidders at Sotheby's, and the average watch bidder spends around USD 129,000, up about 60 per cent year on year. Demand is shifting toward independent makers such as F.P. Journe and Rexhep Rexhepi rather than speculative names.

The Americana collection of the late Jim Irsay totalled USD 105.2 million across five auctions at Christie's finishing on 6 July, the highest total ever achieved for a memorabilia collection. Heritage Auctions has reported a record USD 1.4 billion of sales so far this year.

lead.title: The governess becomes the household's rarest specialist, and the family now recruits half a year ahead to secure one
lead.standfirst: As families compete for a vanishing pool of qualified childcare and education staff, the search for a governess now begins months before she is needed.
lead.body:
The governess, long the quiet centre of the educated household, has become one of the hardest positions in private service to fill. Agencies that place staff for ultra-high-net-worth families report that demand for a formally trained governess, a role distinct from the nanny in its focus on a child's education, languages and cultural formation, now consistently outruns supply. Morgan & Mallet International, which recruits across Europe, the Gulf and the United States, lists governesses among the most requested and least available candidates on its books.

The salaries record the scarcity. In Switzerland, the most generous market, a governess now earns around USD 156,000 and a nanny around USD 144,000, figures that rival those of senior professionals in other fields. In New York a governess commonly commands from USD 50,000 to USD 120,000 depending on languages, travel and whether the post is live-in, while international placements for the most experienced candidates routinely pass USD 200,000. Discretion carries its own premium: agencies estimate that a proven record of confidentiality adds 15 to 20 per cent to a salary.

What families now buy is less a pair of hands than a specialist. The 2026 guidance from household recruiters notes that qualifications increasingly matter more than years served, with STEM-trained nannies and governesses fluent in two or three languages the most sought after. The consequence is a longer hunt. Where a household once expected to fill a post in two to three months, recruiters now advise planning four to six months ahead, and budgeting above the standard rate to secure a candidate at all.

The shortage is structural rather than seasonal. The pool of people willing to live inside another family's private life, to travel at short notice and to hold to exacting standards of privacy, has not grown as fast as the number of households able to pay for them. Every new fortune that hires its first governess draws from the same small pool, and the price of entry rises with each one.
lead.why: For anyone training to run a household, the governess is now among the most valuable and most contested hires a principal will make; understanding how she is found, paid and kept is central to the modern service craft.

articles.title: The ultra-wealthy now hold USD 63.8 trillion, and Altrata maps a USD 26 trillion opportunity moving east
articles.body:
Altrata's World Ultra Wealth Report 2026 puts the combined fortune of the world's ultra-high-net-worth individuals, those worth USD 30 million or more, at USD 63.8 trillion, a sum more than twice the annual output of the United States economy. This narrow band, just 1.1 per cent of the world's dollar millionaires, now commands close to a third of that group's total wealth.

The report frames the coming decade as a USD 26 trillion investable opportunity, the pool of assets this class is expected to put to work as fortunes are managed, transferred and reinvested. Altrata forecasts the ultra-wealthy population will reach 746,570 individuals by 2030, holding some USD 85 trillion, roughly a third more than in 2025.

The centre of gravity is shifting east. Asia recorded ultra-wealthy population growth of 15.8 per cent in 2025 and is projected to grow fastest of the three major regions to 2030. Delhi is forecast to be the fastest-growing city for ultra-wealthy residents over that period, ahead of Stockholm and Wuhan, a reshuffling of the map that will decide where the next generation of great households is built.

One finding tempers the picture of inherited privilege: four fifths of North America's ultra-wealthy are entirely self-made. The service world that grows up around new money differs from the one that surrounds old estates, less bound by inherited staff and settled tradition, more inclined to build a household from nothing.
articles.why: Where the ultra-wealthy multiply, and how their fortunes pass to the next generation, determines where private-service careers will be made over the coming decade.

articles.title: The superyacht order book thins for a second year, and the boats still being built grow larger than ever
articles.body:
The 2026 edition of BOAT International's Global Order Book records 1,093 yachts of 24 metres and above on order or in build, down from 1,138 a year earlier and the second consecutive annual fall by unit count. More than 600 of those hulls are under active construction.

The number of boats has slipped, but their scale has not. The average length of a yacht on order has reached an all-time high of 48.5 metres, as owners commission fewer but larger, more complex and more technically demanding vessels. Italy dominates the industry, building more than 55 per cent of the world's yachts by number, and Azimut-Benetti remains the largest builder by volume.

The most striking hull on the water points to where the market is heading. Project Zero, a 68.85-metre sailing yacht from the Dutch yard Vitters, was conceived as the first superyacht to run entirely without fossil fuels. Demand for sail endures: Southern Wind reports an order book stretching to 2028.

For crew and shore staff the trend matters more than the headline. A fleet of larger, more sophisticated boats needs more, and more specialised, people to run it, from engineers who understand hybrid propulsion to interior teams trained to hotel standard. Fewer launches each year do not mean fewer posts; they mean harder ones.
articles.why: The size and complexity of the boats being built now set the demands on the crews who will run them, a logistical world the private concierge and estate manager increasingly touch.

articles.title: The Birkin proves the strongest asset in the wardrobe, and the rarest examples now trade like fine art
articles.body:
In July 2025 the original Hermes Birkin, the prototype made for the actress and singer Jane Birkin in 1984, sold at Sotheby's in Paris for EUR 8.6 million, around USD 10.1 million, the highest price ever paid for a handbag at auction. The previous record, USD 513,040 for a white Himalaya crocodile Kelly at Christie's Hong Kong in 2021, was left far behind. Bidding opened at EUR 1 million and a private Japanese collector outbid eight rivals.

The sale confirmed a shift collectors had watched for years: the finest Hermes bags now trade less like accessories than like works of art or fine watches, valued for provenance, rarity and condition. Resale specialists describe the Birkin and the Kelly as among the few consumer objects that hold and often increase their value over time.

The momentum has carried into 2026. Heritage Auctions has offered a rare double-signed Birkin estimated at EUR 185,000 to EUR 275,000, while in May a group of white crocodile Birkins seized from the jailed Vietnamese property tycoon Truong My Lan came to sale, the star lot a rhinestone-set Birkin 25 fetching USD 440,144.

For the household, the trend widens the definition of a collection worth cataloguing, insuring and moving with care. The wardrobe has joined the cellar, the watch box and the picture wall as an asset class in its own right.
articles.why: Cultural fluency across the objects a principal collects, from watches and wine to handbags, is part of the service craft; the pieces that appreciate are increasingly the ones a household must protect.

articles.title: Rosewood returns to Crete with the Blue Palace, and the family that wants a private pool has eighty-five to choose from
articles.body:
Rosewood returns to Greece in 2026 with the Blue Palace, a reopened resort on the north-eastern shore of Crete, set between the coastal towns of Plaka and Elounda and looking across the water to the islet of Spinalonga. The property brings 154 rooms and suites under the Rosewood name, 85 of them with private pools.

The proportion is the point. A resort in which more than half the accommodation comes with its own pool is built for guests who want the privacy of a villa with the service of a hotel, the model that increasingly defines top-end travel for families used to running their own estates.

Crete's north-east has long drawn a discreet, returning clientele, and the arrival of a Rosewood raises the ceiling on what the island offers. For the family that takes a cluster of villas for a season, the resort becomes in effect a temporary private estate, staffed and stocked to order.
articles.why: The private-pool villa within a managed resort is the format the travelling household now expects; knowing which properties deliver it is part of planning a principal's summer.

briefs.b: UBS's Global Wealth Report 2026 finds global personal wealth rose 10.8 per cent in 2025, the fastest in three years, adding close to one million new dollar millionaires, about 2,680 a day.
