briefs.b: Round-the-clock close protection now runs on a three-agent rota, and the salary bill alone for that cover reaches from USD 285,000 to USD 375,000 a year in the United States, before travel and equipment. It is why protection now sits on the household ledger beside the estate manager.

The branded-residence pipeline now spans more than 90 countries, with the Middle East and North Africa up 187 per cent in five years. Spa, longevity and dedicated medical services are becoming standard features rather than extras.

A 1964 Shelby Cobra Daytona Coupe carries an estimate in excess of USD 25,000,000 at Gooding Christie's Pebble Beach, the second most valuable lot of Monterey week. It trails only a 1996 McLaren F1 GTR guided above USD 35,000,000.

Amangani, Aman's clifftop lodge above Jackson Hole, has been closed for a full renovation since April 2025 and is due to reopen in late 2026. It returns to a market where trophy properties are running short of peak-season rooms.

lead.title: The cost of living well climbs 10 per cent, and where a family bases itself now decides what its household costs
lead.standfirst: Julius Baer's 2026 index finds the price of a premium life up 10.2 per cent in dollar terms, with Singapore first, Zurich second and Monaco in the top three for the first time.
lead.body:
The Julius Baer Global Wealth and Lifestyle Report, published in Zurich on 7 July, is the private world's closest thing to an annual audit of what an affluent life actually costs. Its Lifestyle Index tracks a basket of 20 goods and services, from residential property and cars to fine dining, watches and schooling, across 25 cities. In 2026 the cost of maintaining that premium standard rose by 10.2 per cent in US dollar terms, a sharp jump that the bank is careful to attribute less to local inflation than to currencies. Money that sits in Swiss francs or euros now buys a great deal more of the world than money anchored to the dollar.

The league table has shifted accordingly. Singapore holds first place for a fourth consecutive year, carried by costly property, expensive cars and a strong local dollar. Zurich climbs three places to second, and Monaco enters the top three for the first time, both lifted by hard currencies and exceptional property prices. Hong Kong slips to fourth and London, a close contender for the top spot a year ago, falls to fifth as the pound tracked the dollar rather than the franc. Europe was the most inflationary region of all, with prices up 14.1 per cent in dollar terms, while Sydney was the year's biggest climber, rising six places to eighth. For the first time in three years no city in the Americas sits in the global top ten.

Some of the steepest rises came in the objects a household is asked to source and insure. With the gold price more than doubling since 2024, jewellery rose 16.4 per cent and watches 15.5 per cent, and luxury goods as a whole climbed 12.3 per cent, outpacing services and reversing recent trends. Behaviour is moving too. At least one in three of the wealthy surveyed have already changed where in the world they buy their luxury goods, more than half would now travel abroad to purchase and sidestep tariffs, and roughly a quarter are already doing so. Health and longevity spending, alongside leisure travel, were the only two categories to rise across every region surveyed.

Running through the whole report is a mood of caution. Between 82 and 95 per cent of respondents in every region said they were concerned or very concerned about geopolitics, and portfolios have turned defensive, with more precious metals, wider geographic spread and higher liquidity. "Currency, once again, is at the forefront," said Christian Gattiker, the bank's head of research, "but it is the interaction between currencies, assets, and behaviour that defines the real story."
lead.why: The house budget is a currency position in disguise. When a principal moves the family seat from London to Zurich or Monaco, the cost of every salary, lease and supplier contract resets, and the manager who can model that shift is worth more than the one who simply pays the invoices.
lead.src: Julius Baer Global Wealth and Lifestyle Report 2026

articles.title: Private jets fly at record levels while their resale market pauses, and the family that flies must read both numbers at once
articles.body:
The business jet market is sending two messages in 2026, and both are accurate. Global business jet departures reached 3.95 million on an April trailing-twelve-month basis, up 4.9 per cent on the year, according to WINGX flight data carried in the JETNET iQ Market Monitor. In the same month, and in the same report, growth in pre-owned aircraft sales cooled from more than 15 per cent as recently as December 2025 to roughly 2 per cent. The sky is busier than ever, yet buyers of second-hand aircraft have grown noticeably careful.

The flying is not spread evenly. Fractional ownership is the standout, expanding 10.0 per cent over the year and 13.0 per cent in April alone, with NetJets now operating around 65 per cent above its pre-pandemic departure levels and Flexjet up 15.1 per cent. Individually owned and shared flying is rising while traditional corporate flight departments retreat, that segment falling 5.9 per cent over the year. For a household, the meaning is plain: the fractional and charter world the family actually relies on is where the pressure on availability is greatest.

The resale hesitation has a clear cause rather than a structural one. Confidence wobbled after a Middle East conflict broke out at the end of February, and monthly transactions turned negative before recovering in April. Average days on the market for a pre-owned aircraft rose to 98, up 11.3 per cent on the year, and the total value of pre-owned deals slipped to 19.25 billion dollars from 20.80 billion for the whole of 2025. Good used aircraft remain scarce, with three quarters of the inventory for sale now 16 years or older, so the family looking to buy well must be patient and precise about the model it wants.

Underneath the noise, demand looks solid. Combined order backlogs across the four largest manufacturers reached 58.2 billion dollars in the first quarter, with Bombardier's book up 43 per cent on the year on appetite for the Global 8000 and Gulfstream's at 22.3 billion. The population of the world's ultra-wealthy climbed to 684,300 in 2025 and is forecast to grow at 5.5 per cent a year to 2028. New aircraft are planned years ahead, which is precisely why the person who arranges the family's travel must think in seasons, not weeks.
articles.why: Aviation is the concierge's hardest logistics problem, and 2026 rewards the one who plans early. Tight used inventory, long delivery queues and record fractional demand mean the family that leaves its lift to the last minute finds the good options already taken.
articles.src: JETNET iQ Market Monitor / WINGX, via Holstein Aviation

articles.title: The wealthy pour money into living longer, and the household is asked to run a private clinic as well as a house
articles.body:
One finding in this year's wealth surveys stands out for the household that serves a principal: spending on health and longevity is rising almost everywhere. Julius Baer's Lifestyle Survey named health, alongside leisure travel, as one of only two categories to grow across every region, confirming what the industry calls the 'health is wealth' shift, in which the affluent increasingly treat longevity as a core part of their fortune rather than a luxury on the side.

The money behind that idea has become enormous. The broader longevity economy was estimated at around 27 trillion dollars globally in 2026, and the narrower market for longevity therapeutics is forecast to reach 314 billion dollars by 2030, growing at more than 25 per cent a year. Roughly 800 longevity clinics now operate in the United States alone, offering full-body imaging, genetic testing, hormone optimisation and regenerative treatments. Entry-level diagnostics can start near 500 dollars, while concierge memberships at the top of the market run to the tens of thousands of dollars a year.

For the private household this is not an abstraction. A principal who has bought into a longevity programme expects the results to shape daily life at home: the chef briefed on a clinic's nutrition protocol, supplements and testing schedules tracked, appointments at specialist centres in Switzerland or California coordinated around the family calendar, and a discreet line kept open to concierge physicians. The house becomes, in part, an extension of the clinic, and the staff are expected to protect the routine as carefully as they protect the family's privacy.

The risk for the profession is credulity. Much of the longevity market is unproven, and the same surveys that record the spending also record deep caution among the wealthy about where they place their trust. The valuable household is the one that can execute a principal's health programme flawlessly while keeping a level head about what it can and cannot deliver.
articles.why: Longevity has quietly become part of the job description. The manager and concierge are increasingly asked to coordinate medical routines, clinics and specialist travel, which demands discretion, precision and the confidence to manage sensitive health logistics without overpromising.
articles.src: Julius Baer 2026 survey; Yahoo Lifestyle longevity clinic report

articles.title: The private governess becomes the household's quiet power, and a candidate-short market pushes pay past USD 150,000
articles.body:
Below the visible senior roles of a great household sits a hire that families guard jealously: the private governess, or governor, who takes charge of a child's education inside the home. Distinct from the nanny, whose remit is care, the governess builds and delivers a curriculum, prepares children for selective schools, and often carries a second or third language into the schoolroom. In 2026 the role has become one of the harder seats in the house to fill.

Recruiters describe a candidate-short market in which qualified, experienced governesses can effectively name their terms. In ultra-high-net-worth households in New York, London and comparable cities, annual compensation now runs broadly from 85,000 to 155,000 dollars gross, with top candidates who hold advanced degrees, multiple languages and a sole-charge academic brief commanding 165,000 dollars or more. International postings, which ask a governess to travel with the family and teach across time zones and residences, carry the highest premiums of all.

The scarcity is a function of expectation. Families increasingly want a single figure who can guarantee continuity of education as the household moves between countries, cover the gap between school terms and tutoring, and hold the academic line without disrupting the child's emotional world. Agencies specialising in the field, from EED to Lighthouse Careers and Eden Private Staff, report that the candidates who combine genuine teaching credentials with the discretion and polish of private service are the rarest of all.

For the estate manager, the governess is both an asset and a delicate management problem. She sits close to the family, often lives in, and shapes the part of the household the principals care about most. Placing the right person, and keeping her, has become a test of a manager's judgement as much as the budget.
articles.why: Education is where a principal's scrutiny is sharpest, and the governess is the household's most sensitive long-term hire. Understanding how the role is defined, priced and retained is now essential knowledge for anyone running a family's staff.
articles.src: Lighthouse Careers Governess Salary Guide 2026; Eden Private Staff

articles.title: A two-speed luxury economy divides the wealthy world, and the household must read which way its principals are leaning
articles.body:
Beneath the headline rise in the cost of living, the Julius Baer survey describes a wealthy world that no longer spends in unison. Consumption has split into what the bank calls a pronounced two-speed luxury economy: spending in Asia Pacific and the Middle East significantly outpaces that in Europe, North America and Latin America, with Europe showing the sharpest contraction of all. The same fortune behaves very differently depending on where it sits.

The divide runs through behaviour as well as volume. Experiential spending dominates in every region, led by luxury hospitality and premium dining, but the confidence to spend freely is concentrated in the East. Asia Pacific investors lead in adapting their portfolios, with 73 per cent increasing diversification, 53 per cent adding precious metals and 46 per cent widening their geographic spread. Middle Eastern investors show a strong appetite for alternatives and collectibles, while Europe leans conservative and preservation-minded and North America reports the steadiest attitudes and the strongest asset growth.

For a household, these are not distant macro trends but signals about the mood of the people it serves. A family whose wealth and outlook are anchored in Asia or the Gulf is more likely to be expanding, acquiring and entertaining; one anchored in Europe may be consolidating and watching costs. The professional who can read that temperature correctly, and calibrate the running of the house to it, is the one who stays a step ahead of instruction rather than a step behind.
articles.why: Household budgets follow their principals' confidence, and that confidence now varies sharply by region. Knowing whether a family sits on the fast or the cautious side of the luxury economy tells a manager whether the year ahead means expansion or restraint.
articles.src: Julius Baer Global Wealth and Lifestyle Report 2026

briefs.t: Gold's surge feeds through to the collection
briefs.b: With the gold price more than doubling since 2024, Julius Baer's index recorded jewellery up 16.4 per cent and watches up 15.5 per cent over the year. For the household that sources, insures and inventories such objects, replacement values and premiums are moving fast, and last year's schedule of cover may already be out of date.
briefs.src: Julius Baer Global Wealth and Lifestyle Report 2026

briefs.t: The wealthy become the market's biggest landlords
briefs.b: Knight Frank's Wealth Report finds private individuals and family offices were the largest buyers of global commercial real estate for a fifth consecutive year, deploying 464 billion dollars in 2025 against 347 billion from institutional investors. The scale of these direct holdings means the modern household increasingly sits alongside a private property operation that also needs managing.

briefs.t: Tokyo leads the world's prime addresses
briefs.b: Knight Frank's Prime International Residential Index recorded Tokyo prime prices surging 58.5 per cent, driven by a weak yen that turned luxury new-builds into a value play for dollar buyers, while global prime prices rose a steadier 3.2 per cent across the 100 markets tracked. For a mobile family, currency now dictates not only what a home costs but where the next one is worth buying.
briefs.src: Knight Frank Prime International Residential Index 2026

lead.title: The private chef becomes the household's most contested hire, and the family now pays a fortune to keep the kitchen
lead.standfirst: Pay for a live-in cook has climbed towards the top of the domestic pay scale as wealthy families compete for a shrinking pool of qualified talent.
lead.body:
The private chef, once a discreet fixture below stairs, has become one of the most fought-over roles in the modern household. Recruiters report that a senior private chef can now earn up to USD 300,000 a year, and that the very top placements, cooking across several residences for a single family, can exceed USD 400,000 once bonuses and allowances are counted. In New York and the Hamptons the working range runs from about USD 130,000 to USD 250,000 and above. In San Francisco it sits between USD 120,000 and USD 200,000. Entry-level placements begin nearer USD 80,000, but the ceiling has risen fast.

The force behind the numbers is scarcity. Demand for private chefs has grown by roughly 35 per cent since 2024, and by close to 18 per cent year on year, with the sharpest appetite for cooks fluent in health-led and specialist dietary work. The supply of candidates who can combine restaurant technique with the discretion, flexibility and travel that a private household demands has not kept pace. A chef who can move between a family's homes, cater a last-minute dinner for thirty and hold a rigorous nutritional brief is rare, and priced accordingly.

Retention has become the deeper problem. Average tenure in these households has fallen from decades to roughly three years, which means families are almost permanently recruiting, onboarding and rebuilding trust. Each departure carries a premium, as principals overpay at the margin to poach a replacement from a rival house. The pay inflation is, in large part, the price of that churn.

The headline salary is only the visible layer. A private chef's package now routinely includes live-in accommodation or a housing allowance, full board, health cover and performance bonuses worth from 7 to 15 per cent of base pay. Total compensation can run from 30 to 50 per cent above the headline figure, and annual increases of 6 to 8 per cent have become the norm for those a family wants to keep. The kitchen, in short, has become one of the most expensive rooms in the house to staff.
lead.why: For a house manager, the chef is the daily heartbeat of the household and its single most visible service. Understanding what the role now costs, and why good cooks leave, is central to building a budget and a team that hold together.

articles.title: The yacht cannot sail without its crew, and in 2026 the qualified crew is the scarcest part of the vessel
articles.body:
As the Mediterranean season reaches its height, the constraint on the world's largest yachts is no longer the hull or the berth but the people who run them. Recruiters describe a persistent shortage of qualified crew, and the shortage is now written into pay. Salaries across the fleet have risen from 8 to 12 per cent since 2023, driven by that scarcity and by inflation, with owners increasingly expected to pay at the top of the range simply to attract and hold experienced hands.

The figures show how far the market has moved. A yacht captain in 2026 earns from about USD 7,000 a month on a smaller vessel to more than USD 25,000 a month on a large superyacht, with senior masters on the biggest hulls paid from EUR 10,000 to EUR 16,000 and beyond. A chief stewardess, the head of the interior and often the guardian of the guest experience, now commands from about USD 5,500 to USD 10,500 a month depending on the size of the yacht, the department she runs and the intensity of the charter calendar.

The pressure is felt most keenly for roles that carry certificates and responsibility. Well-trained stewardesses with strong references, and deckhands who arrive with the correct tickets and a professional attitude, are in steady demand across both private and charter fleets. Owners who once treated crew pay as a rounding error against the cost of the vessel now find that the interior and the bridge are where a season is won or lost.

For the family that owns the yacht, the lesson mirrors the one playing out onshore. The asset is only as good as the team that runs it, and the team is no longer cheap, plentiful or easy to keep.
articles.why: A concierge or estate manager who oversees a family's yacht sits at the centre of this labour market. Knowing what crew now cost, and how hard they are to retain, shapes every conversation about a season afloat.

articles.title: The private members' club is booming again, and the family's access to the right rooms becomes a service in itself
articles.body:
While much of ordinary nightlife struggles, the private members' club is enjoying a conspicuous revival. In London the retailer Selfridges is preparing to open 40 Duke, named for its Duke Street address, with a dining room, a bar and lounge for eighty guests and a terrace seating a further sixty-four. Maslow's, a collection of design-led members' houses, has announced Maslow's Kensington for the spring, and the wellness group Six Senses is trialling its own members' concept, Six Senses Place.

The expansion is not confined to London. The Ned has added a New York house in a 1903 building, and Zero Bond, a fixture of the downtown Manhattan scene, has opened a second location at Wynn Las Vegas. Across both cities, joining fees run into the thousands, and yet the waiting lists lengthen.

The backdrop makes the contrast stark. Britain's Night Time Industries Association counts roughly 16 per cent fewer nightlife venues in London since the pandemic, even as the high-end members' rooms flourish. The trade body's chief executive attributes it plainly to spending power, noting that the clientele of these rooms is making strong money and choosing to spend it behind a controlled door.

For the household that serves a wealthy principal, the club is more than a night out. Access, introductions and the quiet management of memberships have become part of the concierge's remit, and knowing which room a family should be seen in, and how to secure the invitation, is now a genuine skill.
articles.why: The right membership opens doors that money alone cannot, and managing a principal's social access is increasingly part of the private service brief. Fluency in this world is fast becoming expected of the senior concierge.

articles.title: Whisky corrects across the board, and the record still belongs to the rarest bottle in the room
articles.body:
The whisky market has entered a more disciplined phase. In Knight Frank's Luxury Investment Index, whisky fell by 10.9 per cent over the year, one of the sharpest declines among the ten categories the index tracks, even as the index as a whole slipped only 0.4 per cent and effectively held its ground. After the speculative surge of the pandemic years, the correction of 2024 and 2025 has left buyers far more careful about what they acquire.

Yet the very top of the market tells a different story. In January 2026 a single bottle of 1982 Old Rip Van Winkle sold at Sotheby's for USD 162,500, the highest price ever recorded for an American whiskey at auction. The lesson is one of selection over accumulation. Collectors are no longer paying up for anything wearing a limited-edition label, but for genuine rarity, high critical scores and unbroken provenance.

The longer arc remains formidable. Rare bottles have delivered gains of close to 280 per cent over the decade to the mid-2020s, and the Rare Whisky index rose some 478 per cent over five years at its peak. The recalibration of 2026 has not undone those returns so much as reminded the market what actually drives them. A ten-year-old release limited to a few hundred bottles from a revered house now frequently outvalues a high-volume twenty-five-year-old expression.

For the household that keeps a serious cellar, the shift rewards knowledge over impulse. Provenance, storage and the discipline to buy the rare thing rather than the fashionable one have become the marks of a well-run collection.
articles.why: Cultural fluency across wine and spirits is part of the private service craft, and a cellar is an asset to be understood, not just stored. Knowing why one bottle commands a record while the index falls is exactly that fluency.

articles.title: Land holds its value as the wealthy look past the house to the estate, and the rural holding becomes a fortress asset
articles.body:
As financial markets stay unsettled, wealthy families are once again looking to land. Knight Frank reports that average farmland now sits at just under GBP 8,700 an acre, with the best deals still being struck at well over GBP 10,000 an acre. The market has cooled from its fastest pace, but values have proved resilient, and the firm expects them to stay broadly stable through the year.

Much of the caution is political rather than economic. A perception that the government favours heavier taxes on the wealthy has made some buyers, particularly from overseas, reluctant to commit millions to high-value rural property. A partial reversal on inheritance tax has softened the blow: under the revised plan, only farms worth more than GBP 2.5 million, doubled to GBP 5 million for a married couple or civil partnership, will face the charge. Knight Frank sees few early signs that the change will push much more land onto the market in 2026.

The appetite for land sits inside a still-expanding universe of wealth. Knight Frank puts the world's ultra-high-net-worth population, those worth USD 30 million or more, at 713,626, an increase of 162,191 since 2021, with the United States now accounting for around 35 per cent of the total. Each of those fortunes is a potential buyer of the kind of trophy acreage that rarely trades.

The rural estate is not merely an investment. It is a working household with its own staff, its own calendar and its own logistics, from shooting and farming to the management of cottages and grounds. As families widen their holdings from the townhouse to the estate, the demands on those who run them widen with them.
articles.why: Estate management is moving beyond the single residence to working land, and the professional who understands rural operations is increasingly in demand. The fortress asset needs a steward, not just an owner.

articles.title: A Venetian landmark reopens under a new flag, and the grandest address on the lagoon returns to service
articles.body:
One of Venice's most storied addresses has returned. After more than three years closed for restoration, the Danieli has reopened on the Riva degli Schiavoni as Danieli, Venezia, a Four Seasons Hotel, welcoming its first guests at the end of July before its formal reopening later in August. The property had long traded as a Luxury Collection hotel and now operates under Four Seasons in partnership with its Italian owner, Gruppo Statuto.

The restoration was entrusted to the designer Pierre-Yves Rochon, who has reworked the Palazzo Dandolo, built in 1471 as the residence of the noble Dandolo family and a landmark of Venetian Gothic architecture, together with the adjoining Casa Nuova, once the treasury of the Venetian Republic. The hotel opens with 120 rooms and suites, a number that will rise to 168 once the restoration of the Palazzo Danieli Excelsior is complete in 2027. A spa with three treatment rooms, a sauna and a hammam is due to follow later in the year.

For a family planning time in Venice, the reopening restores a benchmark address at the heart of the city, steps from the Doge's Palace and the lagoon. It is the sort of arrival a concierge is expected to know about before the guidebooks catch up.
articles.why: Planning a principal's travel means knowing which addresses have just changed hands or reopened, and why they matter. A landmark returning under a new flag is precisely the intelligence a concierge is expected to hold.

briefs.b: Impressionist and modern art was the standout of Knight Frank's 2026 index, rising 13.6 per cent. The surge was led by Gustav Klimt's Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer, which fetched USD 236.4 million, the highest price ever paid for a modern artwork at auction.

briefs.t: The handbag as a record asset
briefs.b: The collectible handbag remains one of the most resilient categories in the market. In July 2025 Jane Birkin's original Hermes Birkin sold at Sotheby's Paris for EUR 8.6 million, about USD 10.1 million, the highest price ever paid for a handbag at auction.

Watches rose 5.1 per cent in the 2026 luxury index, among the stronger performers. Patek Philippe outpaced the field with a gain of 12.1 per cent, led by demand for the Aquanaut and Nautilus, while the Rolex market index added 4.6 per cent.

The world's ultra-high-net-worth population, those worth USD 30 million or more, has reached 713,626, up 162,191 since 2021. The United States created 41 per cent of the new fortunes and now holds around 35 per cent of the global total.

lead.title: The family office turns cautious, and the household it runs feels every choice it makes
lead.standfirst: UBS finds a record share of the world's largest private offices redrawing their portfolios, and the staff who serve those families sit closest to the consequences.
lead.body:
The family office is the quiet institution behind almost every great household, the entity that pays the salaries, signs the leases, insures the art and decides whether the second home is kept or sold. When it changes course, the people who run the houses feel it first. This year it is changing course more decisively than at any point UBS has measured. In its Global Family Office Report 2026, published on 28 May, the bank surveyed 307 family offices across more than 30 markets, families worth an average of USD 2.7 billion, each office managing an average of USD 1.3 billion. For the first time in the history of the survey, 60 per cent said they plan to alter their strategic asset allocation within the next 12 months, the highest figure UBS has ever recorded.

The mood is defensive rather than adventurous. Geopolitical conflict now ranks as the top risk over both the short and long term, ahead of debt and recession, and the response is diversification rather than bold bets: spreading capital across asset classes, currencies and regions. Sixty-five per cent expect confidence in the US dollar's reserve status to weaken, and many are building multi-currency frameworks around the euro and the Swiss franc. Artificial intelligence remains the single leading theme, with 65 per cent already invested across data centres, software and semiconductors, though even here the language is one of selectivity and resilience rather than exuberance.

For the private-service professional, the most telling section is not about markets at all. UBS found that while family offices have professionalised their investing, with 68 per cent running formal performance measurement and 60 per cent operating investment committees, the human side lags badly. Fewer than half have a formal governance framework with board-level oversight, only 35 per cent have a succession plan for the office itself, and just 27 per cent have a structured process to prepare the next generation. The machinery that manages the money is maturing faster than the family that owns it.

That gap is where estate managers, chiefs of staff and principal private secretaries increasingly earn their keep. When there is no clear succession plan, continuity rests on the people who hold the institutional memory of a house: who the trusted contractors are, how the principal likes to travel, what the last generation promised the long-serving staff. A defensive, diversifying office also means tighter scrutiny of household budgets, more questions about the cost of a second residence or a rarely used yacht, and more pressure on the people who justify those lines. The family that hedges its portfolio tends, sooner or later, to audit its household too.
lead.why: The family office sets the budgets, salaries and priorities of the households that private staff run. When it turns cautious and admits its own succession gaps, the professionals who hold a house together become more valuable, and more closely watched.

articles.title: The order book shrinks in number and swells in size, and the family that wants a new yacht now waits years for a slot
articles.body:
Boat International's Global Order Book, the industry's annual census of what is being built, lists 1,093 yachts of 24 metres and above on order or in construction for 2026, down from 1,138 a year earlier. It is the second consecutive annual fall by unit count, and on the surface it reads like a market cooling. Look closer and the opposite is true at the top. Average length under construction has risen to a record 40.8 metres and average volume to 551 gross tonnes, the highest ever recorded. Fewer boats are being built, but the ones that are being built are the largest in the history of the fleet.

The geography of that construction has consolidated. Italy now accounts for 568 of the yachts on order, 52 per cent of the global total by units, cementing its dominance of the industry. At the very top, the northern European yards that build the giants are effectively full. Trade press reports slot availability at the leading Dutch and German builders extending into 2028 and 2029, with capacity long since committed. A yacht is no longer something a newly wealthy family simply buys; at the largest sizes it is something they queue for.

That scarcity reshapes the work of anyone who serves a yacht-owning family. When new build slots are booked years out, the pressure moves to the charter and brokerage market, where the best large hulls are secured far in advance and the family that decides late finds nothing suitable left. Crew, too, become harder to hold: a shrinking number of new launches means fewer fresh senior positions, and the captains, chief stewardesses and pursers who run these vessels can command more to stay. For the estate manager or private office coordinating a principal's summer, the lesson of the 2026 order book is that time, not money, is the binding constraint.
articles.why: Yachts are the most complex logistical asset a private household manages. A tighter order book and full build slots push scarcity into charter, brokerage and crew, the parts of the yachting world that estate managers and private offices actually touch.

articles.title: Dubai becomes the capital of the ten-million-dollar home, and with each sale a new household is built from nothing
articles.body:
The centre of gravity of the world's most expensive housing has moved to the Gulf. Knight Frank's research on prime residential markets shows global luxury values rose 3.2 per cent in 2025, a shade below the 3.6 per cent of the year before, but the headline masks how uneven the growth has become. The Middle East led the world, and within it Dubai stood alone, recording a 25.1 per cent rise in luxury values and confirming its place as the most active super-prime market on earth.

The numbers at the very top are the ones that matter to anyone who will staff these homes. Dubai closed roughly 500 transactions above USD 10 million in the period, generating around USD 9.05 billion in ultra-luxury sales value, making it the world's number one market for homes at that level. Each of those sales is not merely a property changing hands but a household coming into existence: a residence that will need a manager, a housekeeping team, security, drivers and, often, a private chef, frequently assembled from scratch in a city where experienced private staff are already in short supply.

Knight Frank also identifies a trend that speaks directly to the craft of running a house. Across prime markets, buyers increasingly refuse to absorb renovation risk and are paying up for move-in-ready homes, driving quick transactions on turnkey properties. A family that buys finished and furnished expects the household behind it to be finished too, staffed, provisioned and running smoothly from the first week. Looking ahead, Knight Frank forecasts prime price growth across its 20-city index rising from 1.6 per cent in 2026 to 2.2 per cent in 2027, with Seoul, not a traditional wealth capital, tipped as the strongest performer. The map of where great households are being created is being redrawn faster than the labour market that serves them can follow.
articles.why: Every ten-million-dollar sale is a new household to be staffed and run. Dubai's dominance, and the shift toward turnkey homes, tells private-service professionals where demand for their skills is concentrating and how quickly a house is now expected to be operational.

articles.title: The auction houses rebound on great estates, and the collection, not the single masterpiece, becomes the prize
articles.body:
After three years of soft sales and constant questions about its health, the top of the art market has found momentum again. The major houses reported their strongest first half in years: Christie's took USD 4.5 billion, its best opening six months in five years, Sotheby's a record USD 4.4 billion, Heritage Auctions USD 1.41 billion, its best first half ever, and Phillips saw sales jump 60 per cent to USD 507 million. A Jackson Pollock, Number 7A, 1948, sold at Christie's for USD 157 million, the sort of trophy result that had been conspicuously absent through the downturn.

The more instructive detail is what drove the recovery. Advisers quoted by ARTnews argue that the weakness of 2023 to 2025 was never about vanishing demand but about a shortage of great collections coming to market. This year the estates returned: Christie's was anchored by the S.I. Newhouse collection, Sotheby's by the Robert Mnuchin and Lewis collections. The lesson the trade drew was that in today's market the provenance and coherence of a whole collection matter more than any single lot. The houses themselves emphasised participation over records, with Sotheby's reporting its highest sell-through rate in more than a decade and a record 4.9 bidders per lot.

The wider dynamic is a flight to quality. Collectors have turned away from the speculative contemporary names of the pandemic years toward postwar masters, modern art and categories where supply is genuinely scarce. For the household that stewards a collection, this is a moment that rewards diligence. Realistic estimates and disciplined selling generated the strongest results, and works are increasingly acquired through private sales, lending and advisory rather than the saleroom alone. The staff who catalogue, insure, transport and account for a family's art operate in a market that once again prizes patience, documentation and genuine quality over noise.
articles.why: A family's art is one of the largest and least liquid assets a household oversees. A market rewarding coherent collections, careful provenance and disciplined selling raises the premium on the staff who catalogue, insure and steward those objects properly.

articles.title: The family office fights for its own staff, and the professional seats behind the household grow scarce and dear
articles.body:
The talent shortage that has pushed up wages for estate managers, chefs and nannies runs straight into the office above them. Family offices are struggling to fill their own professional roles, and the data now shows just how expensive the contest has become. According to analysis of Botoff Consulting's 2026 Compensation and Talent Planning Survey, more than a third of family offices reported recruiting difficulties over the past year, with the largest offices reporting the greatest strain.

The money has followed the scarcity. A chief of staff in a family office now commands a median base salary of around USD 320,000, with total compensation near USD 415,000, and New York and San Francisco carry premiums of 15 to 25 per cent over comparable roles elsewhere. The hardest seat to fill is the chief financial officer: strategic, tax-literate professionals with estate-planning experience are described as exceptionally difficult to source, precisely the skills a family needs as wealth passes between generations. Offices are also moving away from discretionary bonuses toward structured, formula-driven pay, a sign of institutions maturing under competitive pressure.

For anyone building a career in private service, this professionalisation matters. The family office is increasingly the ceiling above the household, and the route from running a principal's home to running the office that funds it is becoming better defined and better paid. Most senior hires still arrive through trusted networks, advisers, lawyers, private bankers and former colleagues, rather than open advertisement, which places a premium on reputation and discretion. The same qualities that make an estate manager indispensable, judgment, loyalty and a command of detail, are the ones the office one floor up is now paying record sums to secure.
articles.why: The family office is the career ceiling above the household, and its hiring struggles show where private service is heading. Rising pay for chiefs of staff and CFOs signals both the value of discretion and judgment and a clearer path upward for those who serve a family well.

briefs.b: Morgan Stanley's tracking of the secondary market shows pre-owned watch prices rising for a third consecutive quarter, up 1.9 per cent in the first quarter of 2026, with 25 of 35 brands in positive territory. Patek Philippe has climbed roughly 18 per cent over the year and Rolex around 9 per cent, as cleared inventory and 7 per cent retail price rises since early 2025 steady resale values. For households that hold watch collections, valuations are firming after two lean years.

Knight Frank tips Seoul as the strongest prime residential market of the next two years, forecasting luxury price growth of about 11 per cent in 2026 and 6 per cent in 2027, ahead of every traditional wealth capital. It is a reminder that the map of where great households form is shifting toward Asia, and that private-service demand may follow into cities not usually associated with old money.

A defining feature of prime markets in 2026, Knight Frank reports, is a shortage of move-in-ready homes, with affluent buyers unwilling to absorb renovation risk and paying up for finished, furnished properties that transact quickly. For estate managers, the expectation is clear: a house bought turnkey is expected to be staffed and running from day one.

briefs.t: The dollar question reaches the household
briefs.b: In the same UBS survey, 65 per cent of family offices expect confidence in the US dollar's reserve status to weaken, and many are building multi-currency frameworks around the euro and Swiss franc. As offices diversify the currencies they hold, households that span several countries may find salaries, budgets and payments increasingly denominated and reviewed in more than one currency.

lead.title: The private nanny becomes one of the best-paid hires in the house, and the qualified candidate is now the scarcest of all
lead.standfirst: Salary guides for 2026 place senior career nannies in ultra-wealthy households on pay that rivals the estate manager, and the shortage of trained candidates is the tightest in private service.
lead.body:
For a generation the private nanny sat quietly below the principal roles of the household. That order has been overturned. The salary surveys published for 2026 place senior career nannies working for ultra-high-net-worth families on packages of £95,000 to £140,000 and above, a band that now overlaps with the estate manager and the head of house. The Norland-trained nanny, long the benchmark of the profession, has become one of the most sought-after and most expensive hires a family can make.

The wider market sits a step below that ceiling but has still moved sharply. Most experienced nannies in the United Kingdom now earn between £50,000 and £80,000 a year, with newly qualified live-in roles in London and the South East starting from £40,000 to £55,000. The top of the range, from £120,000 upwards, is reserved for rota and international positions, where two nannies rotate weeks so the household is never uncovered, and where the successful candidate is expected to travel, to speak more than one language and to work seamlessly alongside security and the wider staff.

The pressure is a supply problem before it is a pay problem. The pool of formally trained, discreet, security-aware candidates grows slowly, and it is now being drawn abroad. Dubai and other low-tax jurisdictions are competing hard for English-speaking senior staff, offering tax-free packages and accommodation that a London family struggles to match on cash alone. The result is that families are paying more to recruit and, harder still, to retain.

For the house that gets it right, the nanny is not a peripheral hire but a figure at the centre of the family's trust, present in the most private hours of the day and often the longest-serving member of staff. Recruiting for the role, budgeting for it across several residences and holding on to the right person has become one of the defining tests of how well a modern household is run.
lead.why: For a house or estate manager, the nanny is now a senior recruitment, budgeting and retention challenge, not an afterthought, and a poor hire in the most trusted seat in the house is among the costliest mistakes a principal can make.

articles.title: A record 165,000 of the world's wealthy will move country this year, and the fortune now travels as a portfolio of passports
articles.body:
The Henley Private Wealth Migration Report for 2026 projects that 165,000 high-net-worth individuals will relocate internationally this year, a rise of 16 per cent on the record 142,000 moves recorded in 2025. The figure is the highest the survey has logged, and it confirms that the movement of private wealth across borders has become a permanent feature of the landscape rather than a reaction to any single event.

The destinations are familiar. The United Arab Emirates, the United States, Italy and Switzerland continue to absorb the largest inflows, while the United Kingdom remains the standout loser, shedding wealthy residents at a pace that policy has done little to slow. Most departing British millionaires are heading to those same four destinations, drawn by lighter tax, residence-by-investment routes and the sense of optionality that a second base provides.

The more telling shift is in how the wealthy now think about the move itself. Henley describes a change from the single relocation to the assembly of what it calls sovereign portfolios, collections of residence rights, citizenships and cross-border investments held so that a family can pivot quickly if circumstances change. The emphasis has moved from leaving one country for another to building resilience and contingency into the structure of the family's affairs.

For the people who serve these households, the consequence is concrete. A principal who holds rights in three or four jurisdictions expects the household to function across all of them, which means staff who can travel, who understand the paperwork of multiple residences and who can open, close and run a home at short notice wherever the family chooses to be.
articles.why: The internationally mobile family expects its household to move and operate across several jurisdictions, so multi-country fluency and readiness to travel are becoming baseline expectations of senior private staff.
articles.src: Henley & Partners, Private Wealth Migration Report 2026

articles.title: London's super-prime tenants set records, then press pause as the wealth-tax question hangs over the market
articles.body:
London's super-prime lettings market has just closed its strongest year on record. Agents report a financial year driven by repeat business and a globally diverse client base, with a flagship letting in prime central London agreed at £60,000 a week and landmark country houses changing hands at £14,000 to £17,000 a week. In the South West, one super-prime lettings desk lifted income by 45 per cent and deal volumes by 33 per cent over the same period.

The force behind the surge is tax. With buyers reluctant to absorb stamp duty and the prospect of a mansion tax, and with the abolition of non-domiciled status reshaping the calculus for internationally mobile residents, many of the wealthy have chosen to rent rather than own. Renting preserves the freedom to leave at short notice, and for a client whose plans may change with the next budget, that flexibility has been worth paying a great deal for.

Yet the same caution that fed the rental boom is now cooling it. In the first half of 2026 there were 17 per cent fewer lettings above £5,000 a week in prime central London than in the same period a year earlier. Agents attribute the slowdown to speculation about a possible wealth tax, which has prompted some internationally mobile tenants to hold back and wait for clarity before committing to a London base at all.

The swing from record activity to hesitation inside twelve months captures how quickly the top of the market now reacts to policy signals, and how provisional the presence of a wealthy household in any one city has become.
articles.why: When principals rent rather than buy, and treat a residence as temporary, the way a house is staffed, opened and closed changes, and the estate manager must run a portfolio built for mobility rather than permanence.
articles.src: Knight Frank, Rental Market Adjusts to Reforms and Future Tax Risks

articles.title: The Mediterranean charter season sells out at the top, and the family that books late finds the best hulls already gone
articles.body:
The Mediterranean charter market has tightened again for the summer of 2026, with weekly rates across the region expected to rise by 5 to 12 per cent depending on area and category. A yacht of 30 to 35 metres now commands roughly USD 35,000 to USD 65,000 a week, a 40 to 45 metre vessel USD 60,000 to USD 120,000, and a 50 to 55 metre yacht USD 100,000 to USD 200,000, before fuel, provisioning and taxes are added.

Geography still shapes the bill. France opens at around EUR 80,000 a week with 20 per cent VAT on top, Italy from a similar base with 22 per cent, while Greece and Croatia remain the softer entry points, with charters starting near EUR 15,000 a week under a 13 per cent rate. The gap has pushed a steady stream of demand towards the eastern Mediterranean, where value and cruising ground are easier to reconcile.

The defining feature of the season, however, is scarcity. Availability is tightening fastest for mid-size superyachts with generous beach clubs, water-toy packages and family cabin layouts, and July and August are expected to be almost fully committed for anything above 50 metres by early spring. The family that leaves its booking to the last moment now finds the strongest hulls long gone.

Crew is the quieter constraint behind the numbers. A Mediterranean-wide shortage of experienced crew pushed operating costs up by 15 to 20 per cent in recent seasons, and service quality varies more than it once did, so vetting the specific captain and chef has come to matter as much as choosing the yacht itself.
articles.why: The concierge or house manager who arranges a charter must now plan close to a year ahead and vet the crew as rigorously as the vessel, since a late booking or an unproven captain can undo the whole trip.

articles.title: Bordeaux offers a fine 2025 into a cautious market, and the collector weighs real quality against five years of falling prices
articles.body:
Bordeaux has released its 2025 vintage into one of the most testing markets in a generation. The wines themselves are widely admired, combining the depth of a warm year with freshness, polished tannins and lower alcohol, and the crop is one of the smallest in recent decades. On quality alone, 2025 is a vintage the serious cellar would want to own.

The difficulty is price. There is broad recognition across the trade that releases had to stay close to 2024 levels, with only modest increases at most, if the campaign was to sell at all. Most estates obliged. The conspicuous exception was Cheval Blanc, which released its 2025 futures at EUR 336 a bottle ex-négoce, up 20 per cent on the previous year, and which reached American shelves near USD 473 a bottle thanks to a weak dollar.

Early sales rose on the weak 2024 campaign, with leading merchants describing volumes as up a little, though still below the levels of five years ago. The secondary market gives the reason for restraint. The Liv-ex Bordeaux 500 index, a standard gauge of prices, fell 16.5 per cent over the five years to the end of May 2026, a decline that has taught buyers to treat en primeur as a question rather than a certainty.

With delivery of the 2025s not due until 2028, the collector is being asked to commit capital now for wine that will arrive in three years, into a market that has punished impatience. The vintage rewards those who buy for the cellar and the table, and tests those who buy for the ledger.
articles.why: Wine fluency is part of the private service repertoire, and the household that builds a cellar is judged on patience and timing as much as on the labels it chooses.
articles.src: Decanter, Bordeaux en primeur sales up a little

briefs.t: Business jet deliveries reach a 17-year high
briefs.b: New business jet deliveries jumped almost 15 per cent in the first quarter of 2026, with 162 aircraft handed over worldwide, and IBA forecasts more than 884 deliveries for the full year, up 6.5 per cent. Gulfstream led 2025 with 158 aircraft and USD 10.01 billion in billings, just ahead of Bombardier on 157.

briefs.t: UAE residents turn to contingency planning
briefs.b: Henley & Partners recorded a 41 per cent rise in enquiries from UAE-based individuals between the fourth quarter of 2025 and the first quarter of 2026, with applications for alternative residence or citizenship up 29 per cent. The firm frames it as a phase of diversification and optionality rather than an exodus.

The 2026 private-staff salary guides show compensation pushing higher again across the top of the profession, with the largest rises falling to estate managers, Michelin-trained private chefs and senior career nannies. Competition from Dubai and other low-tax jurisdictions for English-speaking senior staff is a principal driver.
